The ongoing war in Ukraine has drawn international attention to the impact of conflict on global agricultural production and food security. On 6 June 2023, the Kakhovka Dam was destroyed. The loss of this critical agricultural and energy infrastructure has left most farmers on the East bank of the Dnipro River without irrigation in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts. This study develops a multi-sensor Earth Observation framework combining high resolution satellite imagery (Sentinel-2, Landsat) with meteorological data (CHIRPS) and water productivity data (FAO WaPOR), using a semi-supervised machine learning pipeline. Using a rigorous stratified random-sampling approach with photointerpretation, we found pre-war irrigated areas between 2019 to 2021 to be on average 187.94 ± 14.43 kHa, approximately 4% of pre-war baseline cropland and 8% of summer season cropland in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts. In 2022, these numbers contracted to 140.04 ± 17.44 kHa with the expanded occupation of these territories by Russia, seeing an additional decline in 2023 to 74.97 ± 17.84 kHa. Fields in 2023 also exhibited variability in irrigation, ranging from interrupted irrigation owing to the destruction of the Kakhovka reservoir, to those that were sufficiently irrigated with water remaining in the channels. Irrigated areas diminished further in 2024 to 15.95 ± 9.97 kHa, a ∼91% decline from pre-war averages. Based on inspection, formerly irrigated fields before 2023 were either systematically abandoned or converted to winter cropland with lower input requirements by 2024–a pattern that continued into 2025 (total irrigated area 5.76 ± 0.87 kHa). This study demonstrates the power of advanced EO workflows to precisely quantify agricultural transformation and infrastructural failure in ground-truth deficient, high-risk environments.

Climate change, particularly the accelerating trend of global warming, manifests in diverse ways across different geographical regions of the world. While some regions increasingly experience excessive rainfall and flood events, others face prolonged periods of heat and severe drought. Although our study area – the Absheron Peninsula – is located along the western coast of the Caspian Sea, where coastal proximity typically contributes to higher humidity levels, recent observations reveal a distinctly different trend. Despite its coastal position, the region has been experiencing a noticeable intensification of drought conditions over the past two decades. In order to evaluate the ecological consequences of these climatic shifts, our research focused on assessing the impact of climate change on vegetation cover. For this purpose, we employed the Normalized Difference Moisture Index (NDMI) as a key remote sensing indicator for quantifying vegetation moisture content and detecting temporal changes in plant water stress. Satellite data from Landsat 5 TM, Landsat 8 OLI, and Landsat 9 OLI-2 were utilized, covering three benchmark years: 2001, 2013, and 2023. All images were pre-processed, atmospherically corrected, and analyzed to ensure comparability across sensors and time periods. The multi-temporal NDMI analysis clearly demonstrates that vegetation moisture has undergone a significant downward trend. Spatial assessment of NDMI classes shows that areas previously categorized as moderate or high-moisture vegetation in 2001 have progressively transitioned into low-moisture or drought-stressed classes by 2013, with this pattern becoming even more pronounced in 2023. These findings indicate that plant water content in the region has decreased markedly, reflecting both reduced precipitation and rising temperatures associated with climate change. Overall, the results confirm that the Absheron Peninsula is becoming increasingly vulnerable to drought, despite being located in a coastal environment. This highlights the necessity for regional adaptation measures, improved water management strategies, and continued monitoring of vegetation health using satellite-based remote sensing tools. These changes in vegetation moisture reflect not only rising temperatures but also increasing pressure on regional water resources. Reduced soil and plant moisture signals growing water scarcity risks, especially in densely urbanized and coastal environments like Absheron, where freshwater availability is already limited.

Understanding ecosystem service dynamics is essential for effective conservation and sustainable environmental management, particularly in protected areas exposed to increasing environmental pressures from climate variability and anthropogenic activities. This study integrates satellite-derived remote sensing indicators with expert-based assessment to evaluate ecosystem service dynamics in the Surkhan State Nature Reserve, Uzbekistan. Vegetation and surface moisture conditions were assessed using the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and the Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI), derived from cloud-free Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager (OLI) imagery acquired in June 2015 and June 2025. Pixel-wise change detection was applied to identify spatial patterns of vegetation and surface moisture changes between the two observation years. To complement the remotely sensed observations, a structured expert-based assessment was conducted among 35 reserve staff members with professional experience in ecological monitoring, environmental management, and protected-area administration. The questionnaire focused specifically on regulating ecosystem services relevant to the conservation functions of the reserve and used a five-point scoring scale. The results revealed pronounced spatial heterogeneity across the reserve’s mountainous terrain, with stable vegetation and surface moisture conditions prevailing across most areas, while localized zones of vegetation degradation and moisture decline were concentrated on steep slopes and elevated surfaces. The expert assessment was generally consistent with the remotely sensed patterns, particularly in areas characterized by environmental stability and localized ecological variability. Integrating satellite-derived indicators with expert knowledge provides a more comprehensive interpretation of ecosystem dynamics and reduces uncertainties associated with single-method assessments. The proposed integrated framework can support evidence-based conservation planning, adaptive ecosystem management, and targeted monitoring of ecological changes in mountainous protected areas.

Accumulated rainfall, temperature, humidity, and vegetation response form a sequence of environmental signals that can be used to anticipate food availability for bees and improve the planning of beekeeping activities. In this context, this literature review discusses the use of climate data to predict the availability of floral resources in semi-arid regions, considering the influence of meteorological conditions on plant phenology and colony foraging behavior. Historical series of meteorological data allow for the evaluation of not only the total precipitation recorded in a given period, but also the frequency, intensity, duration, and temporal distribution of rainfall—factors that can directly influence processes such as germination, budding, vegetative growth, and the onset of flowering. In semi-arid environments, small differences in rainfall distribution can produce distinct responses in vegetation and significantly alter the availability of nectar and pollen. High temperatures also influence phenological cycles, potentially accelerating certain stages of plant development or reducing flower lifespan when associated with water stress conditions. Soil and air humidity also interfere with plant functioning and can influence nectar production and concentration, altering the attractiveness of flowers to pollinators. The integration of these climate variables with vegetation indices obtained through remote sensing expands the capacity to monitor the actual response of the landscape to meteorological events. Satellite imagery can provide information on changes in vegetation cover, plant vigor, and vegetation recovery after rainy periods, complementing data obtained from weather stations. Statistical models and machine learning techniques can relate climate conditions observed in previous periods to flowering and productivity records, making it possible to build estimates or probabilities of occurrence for specific floral resources in the following weeks. This forecasting capacity has the potential to transform environmental data into information directly applicable to apiary management. For producers, forecasts about periods of greater floral availability can assist in planning strategic feeding, hive migration, super placement, nucleus formation, colony strengthening, and harvest scheduling. However, the literature highlights that a specific amount of rainfall does not necessarily produce the same response in all environments. Soil characteristics, botanical composition, vegetation conservation conditions, plant developmental stages, and species distribution can modify the phenological response after a precipitation event. For this reason, climate data must be combined with information on local phenology and the composition of plant communities existing within the apiaries' area of influence. Another important factor is the spatial scale of meteorological information. Stations located at great distances may not adequately represent conditions in valleys, highlands, higher altitude areas, irrigated regions, or sites with specific relief and vegetation cover characteristics. The creation of regional databases that gather climate, phenological, and productive information allows models to progressively expand their capacity to recognize patterns specific to each territory. Furthermore, monitoring over several years can reveal relationships between different rainfall regimes and the occurrence of blooms, contributing to the identification of periods with greater predictability as well as risk situations. It is concluded that the climate prediction of floral resources is technically viable and holds great potential for beekeeping in the Semi-Arid, especially when different sources of information are used in an integrated manner. Building regional databases and engaging producers in recording blooms can continuously refine models and transform meteorological information into practical tools for decision-making, contributing to greater production efficiency, risk reduction, and the adaptation of beekeeping to the climate conditions of the Semi-Arid. Keywords: Climate data; Prediction; Floral resources; Bees; Semi-arid.

This study was conducted to determine the distribution area and estimate the carbon stock of the seagrass ecosystem in Con Dao Island through the application of remote sensing technology, GIS, and the Google Earth Engine platform. The study used Sentinel-2 Level-2A satellite imagery acquired from January 2025 to July 2025 in combination with field survey data. The satellite imagery was processed on the Google Earth Engine platform through cloud masking, multi-temporal image compositing, and the calculation of spectral indices, including NDVI and NDWI. The Random Forest algorithm was applied to classify marine surface cover and identify the distribution extent of seagrass beds. The training dataset consisted of three main classes, namely seagrass, sand, and water, with a total of 106 samples, of which 70% were used for model training and 30% for model validation. The results showed that the classification model achieved an overall accuracy of 88.24% and a Kappa coefficient of 0.810, reflecting the high reliability of the applied method. The total seagrass area in Con Dao after field verification was estimated at approximately 999.08 ha, mainly distributed around Con Son, Bay Canh Island, and Mui Chim. Based on five field biomass samples and the carbon conversion coefficient recommended by the IPCC (2006), the study estimated that the total carbon stock accumulated in seagrass biomass was approximately 13,196.73 kgC. The findings of this study provide an important scientific basis for marine resource management, seagrass ecosystem conservation, and the future development of blue carbon credit initiatives in Con Dao.

Abstract. In the context of climate change and the growing need for improved observations of the atmospheric water cycle, measurements of atmospheric water vapor over the global ocean remain scarce compared with those available over land. This observational gap can be addressed using Integrated Water Vapor (IWV) derived from shipborne Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) observations, which provide a robust and well-established method for monitoring atmospheric moisture over the oceans. This study presents a shipborne IWV dataset obtained from the processing of raw data collected by GNSS antennas installed on research vessels. The dataset benefits from substantial support and data access provided by Genavir, the operator of the French Oceanographic Fleet (FOF), and the Ifremer archive department SISMER. It is based on oceanographic campaigns conducted worldwide by eight vessels over a ten-year period (2015–2024), representing a total of 6,427 campaign days in both offshore and coastal regions. After describing the methodology used to derive IWV from raw GNSS observations and to remove spurious measurements through a screening procedure, the dataset is evaluated through comparisons with the ERA5 reanalysis and satellite radiometer measurements from Remote Sensing Systems. These comparisons yield mean differences of (0.3 ± 2.0) kg m−2 and (−0.4 ± 1.8) kg m−2, respectively. To further quantify the inherent uncertainty of the shipborne IWV retrieval, the dataset is cross-validated using instances where two vessels were within 50 km of each other. This comparison results in an estimated uncertainty of 0.96 kg m−2, demonstrating the suitability of the dataset for climate studies. Local discrepancies identified in these comparisons are discussed, highlighting limitations in each dataset considered. The GNSS-derived IWV dataset is intended to be updated annually to support long-term monitoring of atmospheric water vapor over the global ocean. The IWV estimates are available at https://doi.org/10.25326/876 (Panetier and Bosser, 2026) through the AERIS data center (https://en.aeris-data.fr/, last access: 20 March 2026), and currently span the period from 2015 to the end of 2024.

The GNSS-derived IWV dataset is intended to be updated annually to support long-term monitoring of atmospheric water vapor over the global ocean. The IWV estimates are available at https://doi.org/10.25326/876 (Panetier and Bosser, 2026) through the AERIS data center (https://en.aeris-data.fr/, last access: 20 March 2026), and currently span the period from 2015 to the end of 2024.

The article presents an overview of modern studies of pasture ecosystems in the arid zone of Southern Kazakhstan using the example of the Otyrar district of the Turkestan region. The article examines the region's natural and climatic features, and the influence of aridization and climate change on the structure of pasture phytocenoses, their productivity, and biodiversity. The main factors of sustainability of pasture ecosystems were analyzed, including water regime, soil salinity, organic carbon content, the state of the soil microbiome, and anthropogenic load. The purpose of this review article is to analyze and summarize recent scientific research on the state, functioning, assessment methods, and prospects for the restoration of pasture ecosystems in the arid zone of Southern Kazakhstan, using the example of the Otyrar district of the Turkestan region. Particular attention is paid to modern methods of geobotanical assessment of vegetation, determination of projective cover, productivity, and biodiversity indicators, as well as to the use of geographic information systems, remote sensing, and satellite monitoring to assess the condition of pastures. The data on the prospects for the restoration of degraded pastures through the use of organomineral fertilizers based on natural aluminosilicates, humic substances, protein hydrolysate, and microalgae Chlorella vulgaris are summarized. It has been shown that an integrated approach combining geobotanical, soil-ecological, and digital research methods contributes to increasing the sustainability of pasture ecosystems, preserving biodiversity, and rational use of natural forage resources in arid territories.

Abstract Root zone water storage capacity () sets the lower limit on the water available to plants and is critical for modeling terrestrial water and carbon fluxes. Due to subsurface heterogeneity in soils, roots, and geology, in‐situ measurements of are infeasible at regional to global scales. Instead, is often estimated using a water balance approach—calculating the difference between precipitation and evapotranspiration to approximate water deficits. This method can be applied using diverse data sets, including those from eddy covariance, satellite remote sensing, reanalysis, and land surface model outputs. However, each data product contains its own uncertainties, and the influence of data set choice on estimates has not been quantified. In this study, we assess the uncertainty in estimates across 90 FLUXNET sites in the continental United States with at least 5 years of data, comparing results from six different precipitation and evapotranspiration data sets. We find substantial variation in estimates across data sets, sites, and land cover types, with particularly high uncertainty for values exceeding 500 mm. Much of this uncertainty can be attributed to differences among evapotranspiration products rather than random errors. Our analysis shows that single data set approaches to quantifying underestimate the variability that emerges when multiple data sets are considered, especially in the Western US. These results underscore the need to account for data‐driven uncertainty when estimating subsurface water storage and provide a foundation for improving model parameterizations of ecosystem drought response and land‐atmosphere interactions.

The article examines the issues of monitoring water fund lands and delineating protection zones of water cadastre objects based on geoinnovative approaches. The study analyzes the possibilities of using geographic information systems (GIS), remote sensing data, satellite imagery, and modern geodetic technologies. The importance of geoinnovative technologies in systematically monitoring the territorial condition of water fund lands, determining the boundaries of water bodies, assessing anthropogenic impacts, and promptly identifying changes is substantiated. In addition, the scientific and practical aspects of using digital cartographic data to delineate water protection zones and sanitary protection areas around water cadastre objects are considered.

The current stage of development in spaceborne Earth remote sensing (ERS) is characterized by the expanding use of ERS data and the improvement of observation systems. Therefore, an important task in designing a promising satellite ERS system is to identify the current requirements for data characteristics: the spatial resolution, imaging frequency, and swath width. This article identifies the requirements for ERS data characteristics necessary to address a wide range of agricultural and forestry tasks. Based on an analysis of the relevant scientific literature, tasks addressed using ERS were listed and divided into six groups of agricultural tasks (mapping and classification, crop and soil/water resource monitoring, forecasting and planning, precision control, regulatory policy oversight, and economic and insurance tasks) and six groups of forestry tasks (forest inventory, forest condition and dynamics monitoring, forest exploitation control, firefighting, scientific research, and planning support). For each group, peer-reviewed scientific publications were selected, which contain specific quantitative requirements for the ERS data characteristics. Based thereon, requirements were identified for optical, thermal, and radar spaceborne imagery. It was shown that, for the overwhelming majority of agricultural and forestry tasks to be resolved, it is sufficient to use optical data with a spatial resolution of 2 to 3 m and a temporal resolution of 2 to 3 days, radar data with a spatial resolution of 3 to 5 m and a temporal resolution of 3 to 6 days, and thermal imagery with a spatial resolution of 20 m and a temporal resolution of 3 to 5 days. The most stringent requirements for spatial resolution are imposed in tasks of early detection of weeds and plant pests. Fighting forest fires requires the highest temporal resolution of thermal imaging: 15 to 30 minutes.

Abstract Monitoring changes in the land surface is an essential element for assessing the transformation processes of the urban and peri-urban environment, especially in regions with a long history of mining activities. The development of Earth observation programs and the availability of freely accessible satellite images allow for detailed multi-temporal analyses of the evolution of vegetation, humidity and the general condition of the land. In this context, spectral indices calculated from satellite images provide objective information on spatial and temporal changes of the analyzed surface. The paper presents a multitemporal analysis of the Petroșani municipality using four of the most widely used spectral indices in remote sensing: Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI), Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR), and Soil Adjusted Vegetation Index (SAVI). The analysis was carried out for the period 2020–2025 based on a set of 20,000 points uniformly distributed in the study area, for each year analyzed. The working methodology included processing the time series of spectral indices, calculating descriptive statistical parameters, comparing annual distributions, analyzing correlations between indicators and interpreting the spatio-temporal trends highlighted during the analyzed period. The integrated approach allows for the simultaneous assessment of vegetation changes, moisture conditions and land surface transformations. The results obtained highlight the existence of interannual variations in all analyzed indices, reflecting both the influence of climatic conditions and the effects of anthropogenic transformations specific to a city in a continuous process of economic restructuring and urban regeneration. The comparative analysis demonstrates the complementarity of the four indices and the usefulness of their integrated use in assessing the evolution of the urban environment. The study confirms that multitemporal analysis based on satellite images is an effective method for environmental monitoring in mining regions and can provide useful information for territorial planning, green space management and the substantiation of sustainable development strategies.

Community-based environmental organizations require continuous water quality data but are constrained by the cost and labor of physical sampling. Satellite remote sensing offers a free alternative, yet validation studies of inland waters frequently report weak agreement between satellite indices and ground measurements, and the cause of that disagreement is rarely isolated. This study analyzed 28 Sentinel-2 observations across 12 dates at three sites on the Buriganga River in Dhaka, Bangladesh, between January and April 2026, alongside eight calibrated field measurements of turbidity, pH, and dissolved oxygen. Three findings emerged. First, the reach adjacent to the Hazaribagh tannery district was more turbid than the Katashur Outfall on every one of 11 valid observation dates (Wilcoxon p = .001), establishing a persistent spatial gradient that discrete sampling campaigns had not resolved. Second, turbidity rose by 88% river-wide between January and February (p = .006), and the cleanest site deteriorated fastest, compressing the gradient between the tannery reach and the outfall from 2.0 to 1.5. Third, repeat same-day observations established a measurement noise floor 2.6 times smaller than between-date variation, indicating that 86% of observed variance reflects genuine day-to-day change. That last result predicts, and the data confirm, that pairing protocol governs retrieval accuracy: comparing generalized field averages against satellite observations from the same approximate period yielded no significant relationship (R² = .04, p = .46), whereas matching each field measurement to a cloud-free overpass on the same calendar date yielded strong agreement (R² = .94, 95% CI [.71, .99], n = 8, p < .001), with a cross-validated retrieval error of 5.4 NTU. Sensor capability was identical under both protocols. Weak validation outcomes in dynamic inland waters may therefore reflect protocol failure rather than sensor limitation.

A key aspect of current developments in Earth observation is the ability to extract additional physical information from measurements through innovative sensor concepts. Polarimetric observations provide an important example. The contribution from Smith et al. presents the Hyper-Angular Rainbow Polarimeter 2 (HARP2), deployed on NASA's Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) mission. In addition to measuring aerosols, the instrument provides highly accurate, multi-angle polarized observations of clouds and is particularly sensitive to the polarized cloudbow produced by liquid-water cloud droplets. The angular structure of this feature contains information on cloud droplet size distributions, allowing the retrieval of effective radius and variance. With a spatial resolution of approximately 5 km and a wide observational swath, HARP2 enables these measurements on a global scale. Its capabilities demonstrate how targeted instrument design can provide new links between cloud microphysics and radiative properties and thereby open new avenues for investigating the role of clouds in the Earth system.The scientific potential of multi-angle polarimetry is further illustrated by the application of cloud tomography to observations from the Research Scanning Polarimeter (RSP). Alexandrov et al. demonstrate the retrieval of two-dimensional distributions of cloud extinction from real airborne measurements acquired during the Cloud, Aerosol and Monsoon Processes Philippines Experiment. The tomographic approach combines information on cloud geometry and directional cloud optical thickness with mathematical inversion techniques to reconstruct the internal structure of clouds. When combined with droplet size information obtained from polarized measurements, the retrieved extinction fields can be related to droplet number concentration. Comparisons with coincident lidar and cloud-radar observations provide an important basis for evaluating the retrievals. Beyond the specific application, this work demonstrates how advanced measurement geometries and inverse methods can transform remote sensing observations into spatially resolved information about processes occurring inside clouds.Innovation in Earth observation also extends to fundamentally different approaches to image acquisition. The Falcon Neuro mission explores the use of event-based vision sensors installed on the International Space Station to detect lightning and related atmospheric electrical discharges. Lightning is characterized by rapid temporal evolution, creating demanding requirements for both spatial and temporal sampling. The study from McHarg et al. demonstrates that event-based sensors provide an alternative to conventional frame-based imaging by responding to changes in the observed scene. Initial measurements demonstrate the potential of this technology for space-based lightning observations. This contribution highlights the opportunities offered by emerging sensor technologies and illustrates how concepts initially developed for other applications can be adapted to address specific challenges in Earth system observation.Another important direction is the optimization of how measurements are acquired. For satellite observations of atmospheric carbon dioxide and methane, clouds can lead to the rejection of a large proportion of measurements. Rather than addressing cloud contamination exclusively after data acquisition, the paper from Nassar et al. investigates the use of real-time cloud information to guide instrument pointing. Simulations of such an "intelligent pointing" strategy show that substantial improvements in the fraction of cloud-free observations can be achieved, particularly for missions in highly elliptical or geostationary orbits. The analysis further demonstrates that field-of-view geometry plays an important role in observational efficiency, with imaging Fourier transform spectrometers offering advantages for scanning irregularly shaped land areas. These findings point toward a more adaptive approach to satellite observations in which environmental information is used to optimize measurements in real time.The work from Gilerson et al. emphasizes another fundamental requirement for successful Earth observation: the rigorous characterization of measurement uncertainty. Uncertainties in oceancolor remote sensing reflectance directly affect the retrieval of chlorophyll-a concentrations and other water properties. An analysis of measurements from the Sentinel-3A and -3B Ocean and Land Colour Instrument (OLCI) shows that, consistent with findings for other ocean-color sensors, spectral components from Rayleigh scattering and surface effects constitute a major source of uncertainty. Variability associated with water-leaving reflectance is also important in coastal regions, while contributions from aerosols and glint are comparatively smaller. The results emphasize that improvements in satellite data products depend not only on sensor performance but also on a detailed understanding of atmospheric correction, radiometric uncertainties, and the characteristics of different observing environments.Viewed together, the contributions demonstrate the breadth of technological and methodological advances currently shaping space-borne Earth observation. They encompass novel polarimetric instrumentation, tomographic retrieval techniques, event-based imaging, adaptive observation strategies, and systematic uncertainty analysis. Importantly, these developments address different stages of the observation chain: from how measurements are acquired, through how instruments are operated, to how observations are interpreted and their accuracy assessed. This combination of technological innovation and methodological development will become increasingly important as satellite missions evolve toward more complex and integrated observing systems. Future instruments are likely to provide measurements with greater angular, spectral, spatial, and temporal information, while increasingly autonomous observation strategies may allow missions to respond dynamically to changing environmental conditions. At the same time, the growing diversity of observations will make robust calibration, validation, uncertainty quantification, and physically based retrieval methods essential for ensuring that increased data volume translates into increased scientific knowledge.The contributions assembled in Instruments and Technologies for Earth Observation Satellite Missions thus provide examples of both current capabilities and future directions in satellite remote sensing. They demonstrate that advancing Earth observation is not simply a matter of developing more sensitive instruments or acquiring more data. Progress also depends on designing measurements around the physical information sought, exploiting innovative observation concepts, optimizing the use of available measurement opportunities, and establishing the accuracy and limitations of the resulting products. Together, these advances will strengthen the ability of Earth observation satellite missions to provide the reliable, detailed, and globally consistent information needed to understand and monitor our changing planet.

Study region The Bosten Lake Basin, located in Northwest China, serves as a regional water resource distribution hub, a crucial ecological barrier, and a major source of water for the Tarim River. Study focus The Bosten Lake Basin is characterized by complex topography and heterogeneous surface conditions, while its glacial environment is highly sensitive to climatic variability. These characteristics make the basin particularly susceptible to climate-driven changes in glacier dynamics. However, reliable estimates of glacial change in this area remain insufficient due to the complexity of debris-covered glaciers and the persistent cloud cover that limits the availability of remote sensing data. To address these challenges, this study develops a classification framework that combines hierarchical object-based methods with rule-based analysis. By integrating multi-source remote sensing data with detailed topographic information, this approach enables the separation of objects with similar spectral signatures. The multi-level classification provides new insights into the spatiotemporal dynamics of glaciers in the Bosten Lake Basin. New hydrological insights for the region The findings reveal a significant decline in glacierized water area across the Bosten Lake Basin, accompanied by increasing fluctuations, highlighting pronounced spatial and temporal heterogeneity in glacier dynamics. Between 2010 and 2025, the total glacier area in the Basin decreased by 880.309 km². This decline occurred in three phases: 432.279 km² from 2010 to 2015, 220.553 km² from 2015 to 2020, and 227.477 km² from 2020 to 2025. Glacier retreat varied markedly with slope orientation, with the most pronounced losses occurring on southern and eastern slopes. This spatial heterogeneity was closely associated with regional variations in precipitation and solar radiation. By applying a multi-level object-oriented and rule-based classification, this study effectively captures the complex glacial environment of the basin. These findings not only document patterns of glacial change but also enhance understanding of the broader environmental consequences of climate change in one of Central Asia’s most sensitive regions.

Tropical peatland degradation remains a critical environmental challenge in Southeast Asia, yet operational monitoring frameworks that align with governance boundaries remain limited. This study aimed to develop an open-data remote sensing framework for assessing peatland condition at the Peat Hydrological Unit (Kesatuan Hidrologis Gambut, KHG) scale in South Sumatra, Indonesia. Using Google Earth Engine, four satellite-derived indicators were extracted annually for 12 KHGs over seven years from 2018 to 2024: Normalized Difference Water Index from MODIS MOD09A1, Enhanced Vegetation Index from MODIS MOD13Q1, fire frequency from NASA FIRMS, and surface water extent from the JRC Global Surface Water dataset. The indicators were normalized and integrated into a weighted composite score using weights of 30% for NDWI, 25% for EVI, 30% for inverse fire frequency, and 15% for surface water extent. In 2024, seven KHGs were classified as At Risk and five as Intact/Recovering, with scores ranging from 46.5 to 76.9. Six KHGs declined between 2018 and 2024, while five improved. El Nino years reduced health scores by an average of 11.3 points, and cropland conversion was the strongest land-cover predictor of lower scores (r=−0.52). Weight sensitivity analysis showed that seven of twelve KHG classifications remained stable across five weighting scenarios. The framework was reproducible, governance-aligned, and suitable as a screening tool for peatland restoration prioritization.

The efficient monitoring of inland water bodies such as rivers and lakes is crucial not only for ensuring human health and ecosystem balance, but also for the effective management of water resources. Two water quality variables of high importance and interest are Dissolved Oxygen (DO) and pH. The former variable is an ecosystem health index as it is connected to hypoxia events, while the latter one is linked to biochemical processes and the acidity of water. Currently, conventional water quality monitoring methods (e.g., via in-situ point sampling) are accurate for the particular point, but costly and time-consuming. On the other hand, satellite remote sensing provides a remedy, as it offers high spatial and temporal coverage. Most of the water quality applications of remote sensing data have focused on optically active parameters like Chlorophyll-a and Colored Dissolved Organic Matter (CDOM), but the estimation of non-optically active variables such as pH and DO poses a significant challenge. This study introduces a novel approach, that fuses Earth Observation (EO) and in-situ data, in a deep learning context, to provide estimations of non-optically active variables, characterized by high accuracy, high spatial coverage and low latency. The approach also considers the data imbalance challenge, which is common in environmental datasets. The approach is applied to Lake Yliki in central Greece. The Boeotikos Kifissos river basin, which lies upstream of Lake Yliki, is dominated by intense agricultural activity. The lake is also part of Athens’ water distribution system, making its efficient monitoring even more important.

Abstract. Within VITAL I, a two-week data-set of novel types of Atmospheric Boundary Layer (ABL) profilers, that are being considered for the next-generation German Meteorological Service DWD observational network is made available. The data set is thoroughly tested and evaluated in the context of the WMO Rolling Requirements Review for short-term / high-resolution weather forecasting. VITAL I took place in August 2024 at the Jülich Observatory for Cloud Evolution JOYCE, which is a National Facility of the ACTRIS European Research Infrastructure Consortium. VITAL I is a core activity of the Hans Ertel Centre for Weather Research, a joint research initiative between German atmospheric research institutions and the German Meteorological Service DWD. Vertical profiling data sets of temperature, humidity and wind using multi-copter uncrewed aerial systems and the ground-based remote sensing profilers Doppler lidar, water vapor lidar and microwave radiometer were created and evaluated against radiosondes and data from a 120 m meteorological tower. Comparisons were also carried out against satellite sounders. Most tested ground-based systems are shown to fulfill the WMO RRR breakthrough requirements and are suited for capturing the diurnal cycle of the ABL. VITAL I also encompassed an international summer school that was simultaneously held at JOYCE to educate students from the Bachelor to PhD level in Modern Methods in Atmospheric Profiling. Data measured during VITAL I is available via https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22960530, (Löhnert et al., 2026).

The research examines the spatiotemporal change of water bodies in Ahmedabad city in western part of India which is a rapidly urbanizing area. It integrates high-resolution remote sensing data with modern machine learning approaches. Understanding the long-term pattern is crucial to understanding and managing the water resources in the changing climate, also city experiences the low precipitation with long summer months that makes managing water resources more challenging. The study utilizes the Landsat-8 imagery from 2013 to 2024 to indices that highlights the water signatures. Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI) and Modified Normalized Difference Water Index (MNDWI) are computed using green, near infrared and mid-infrared Landsat bands. Machine learning classifier algorithms are used to identify the water area and non-water area pixel. The selected algorithms are classification and regression trees (CART), minimum distance (MD), naïve bias (NB) and random forest (RF) for that training data points are collected with visual inspection of available satellite images and manual in-situ inspection. Train and testing data is split in 80-20 to train and validate the classification of water area. A time series are generated for 12 years in both monthly and yearly scale. The primary objective is to assess the water area changes across the past decade, changing water area due to the anthropogenic impacts and climatic factors effect on it due to abrupt changing climate. Furthermore, the study attempted to provide a systematic approach to analysis the water area changes and patter identification that will be useful for policy making on water resource management for the city. The study demonstrates the essential requirement for data-driven governance of water resources, providing insights into sustainable urban development and environmental conservation strategies aligned with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 6 and 11, which focus on clean water and urban sustainability. Based on the analysis of the water area time series a slight upward trend is evident with both yearly and monthly tread with Mann-Kendall test across all the classifiers. Temperature has significantly driver of water change and precipitation has low impact in the long-term water area change. CART and Naïve Bayes showed better performance, with CART being linearly sensitive to temperature and others exhibiting non-linear precipitation dependencies. The deployed machine learning models underscoring the effectiveness of combining remote sensing with machine learning. The research enhances hydrological monitoring and ongoing environmental evaluations by adeptly combining traditional remote sensing methods with modern computational methodologies.

Coral reefs in the Caribbean Basin, including Puerto Rico's, are severely threatened by various factors such as overfishing, high sea surface temperatures (SSTs) leading to bleaching, and diseases. Critically, land-based sources of pollution (LBSP) remain a major local and regional threat. To sustain healthy coral reefs, baseline water quality data is essential for scientific and management perspectives. Coral reef health depends on acclimation to water quality parameters like light, temperature, dissolved oxygen, and oligotrophic (low-nutrient) conditions. The Problem: Comprehensive water quality assessments in Puerto Rico's coral reef environments are limited, which hinders informed decisions for restoration projects. Long-term monitoring is needed to provide data for events (e.g., wastewater and sediment runoff) that can cause coral disease and mortality. The Solution: Local stakeholders agree that characterizing water quality patterns through quantitative and qualitative data is necessary for advancing coral restoration. The Program Design: This program was designed as a sustainable, island-wide initiative to monitor long-term water quality conditions and trends in shallow coral reefs across Puerto Rico. It integrates: Diverse water quality datasets. State-of-the-art satellite-derived methods (remote sensing) and in situ observations. Recommendations for implementation. The goal is to monitor long-term exposure and trends, as previous studies have not adequately evaluated the chronic exposure of coral reefs to degraded water quality.This program was further summarized in the Puerto Rico Coral Reef Water Quality Program Storymap and the Puerto Rico Coral Reef Water Quality Program Summary.

The article develops a cloud-based workflow for preliminary cadastral monitoring of agricultural lands in Almaty Region using Google Earth Engine and the Random Forest algorithm. The study focuses on the remote-sensing diagnosis of actual land-surface conditions rather than on potential land suitability assessment. Landsat 8/9 Surface Reflectance images were processed for 2015, 2020 and 2025, and Sentinel-2 imagery was used as an auxiliary visual reference for sample interpretation. Seasonal composites were generated, cloud-contaminated pixels were masked, and NDMI and BSI indicators were calculated to describe moisture-related conditions and exposed or sparsely covered surfaces. The spectral bands and derived indicators were then combined in a Random Forest classifier to distinguish four monitoring classes: stable vegetation cover, open or sparsely covered soil, water bodies, and built-up or non-agricultural areas. Validation was performed using an independent sample, and class areas were calculated from the classified raster. The resulting map is proposed as a diagnostic layer for identifying territories that may require additional cadastral or field verification. The approach does not replace official cadastral records, but it supports land-use control through reproducible satellite-based evidence.

Актуальность работы. Русловые водохранилища Юга России на всем протяжении своего существования подвергаются значительным изменениям за счет интенсивной переработки берегов, заиления и зарастания. Выполнение своевременной оценки степени происходящих изменений в условиях масштабной антропогенной нагрузки региона, климатической нестабильности и дефицита регулярных наземных наблюдений является важной и актуальной задачей. К числу наиболее динамичных участков берегов водохранилищ относятся заливы, образовавшиеся в результате затопления русел и долин боковых притоков главной реки подпором созданного водохранилища. Трансформация таких заливов зависит от суммарного влияния гидрологических, физических, морфологических, биологических и других доминирующих факторов. Цель работы заключается в обосновании и разработке структуры комплексного мониторинга современного геоэкологического состояния крупных заливов за последнее десятилетие. Методы исследования. В основу разрабатываемых методов положена бассейновая концепция природопользования, которая признана наиболее важным и эффективным методом территориальной организации мониторинга. Применительно к заливам водохранилищ использование этой концепции позволяет выявить взаимосвязи и взаимозависимости частей единой геосистемы «водосбор–водоток–устье–залив–приемный водоем». Особое влияние на формирование экологического состояния заливов оказывают не только разновременные и разнонаправленные колебания уровня водохранилища, но и режим и качество речного стока, характер и интенсивность антропогенной нагрузки на водосбор. Разработка содержания информационных блоков мониторинга осуществлялась с применением дистанционных и картографических методов на основе ГИС-технологий. Результаты. Разработана структура блоков комплексного мониторинга заливов русловых водохранилищ и апробирована методика их информационного наполнения на примере заливов Цимлянского водохранилища. В данной статье приводятся результаты исследований, выполнявшихся для Новоцимлянского залива и водосборов впадающих в него рек Цимла и Россошь за период 2015‒2025 гг. на основе совместного использования спутниковой информации, картографических материалов, ГИС-технологий, данных Донского бассейнового водного управления (БВУ) и экспертных оценок. Основным источником информации являлись многолетние данные искусственных спутников Земли (ИСЗ) Sentinel-2А, Sentinel-2В, Landsat-8,9. С помощью расчетных спектрозональных индексов (водных и вегетационных) получены данные о многолетних изменениях площади зеркала воды залива и динамике его зарастания. По разновременным снимкам прослежено изменение границ зон переменного подпора залива при максимальных и минимальных годовых изменениях уровня водохранилища Relevance. Channel-type reservoirs of Southern Russia have undergone substantial transformations throughout their existence as a result of intensive shoreline reworking, sedimentation, and overgrowth by aquatic and semi–aquatic vegetation. Timely assessment of the magnitude and direction of these changes under conditions of strong anthropogenic pressure, climatic instability, and a lack of regular in situ observations is a critical and highly relevant task. Among the most dynamic shoreline segments of reservoirs are bays formed by the inundation of channels and valleys of lateral tributaries of the main river due to backwater effects caused by reservoir impoundment. The transformation of such bays is governed by the combined influence of hydrological, physical, morphological, biological, and other dominant factors. Objective. The objective of this study is to substantiate and develop the structure of an integrated monitoring system for assessing the current geoecological condition of large reservoir bays over the past decade. Methods. The proposed methodology is based on the basin–oriented concept of nature management, which is recognized as one of the most effective approaches to the territorial organization of environmental monitoring. When applied to reservoir bays, this concept makes it possible to identify interconnections and interdependencies between components of the unified geosystem “catchment-main river-estuaries-reservoir”. The ecological condition of reservoir bays is strongly influenced not only by asynchronous and multidirectional water–level fluctuations of the reservoir, but also by the regime and quality of river runoff, as well as the nature and intensity of anthropogenic pressure within the catchment area. The development of the monitoring information blocks was carried out using remote sensing and cartographic methods based on GIS technologies. Results. A structured system of integrated monitoring blocks for bays of channel–type reservoirs was developed, and the methodology for their informational content was tested using the bays of the Tsimlyansk Reservoir as a case study. This paper presents the results of studies conducted for the Novotsimlyansky Bay and the catchments of the Tsimla and Rossosh rivers discharging into it over the period 2015–2025. The analysis was based on the combined use of satellite imagery, cartographic materials, GIS technologies, data from the Don Basin Water Authority, and expert assessments. The primary data sources were long–term satellite observations from Sentinel-2A, Sentinel-2B, and Landsat-8/9. Calculated multispectral indices (water and vegetation indices) were used to quantify long-term changes in the bay’s water surface area and the dynamics of its overgrowth. Multitemporal imagery enabled tracing changes in the boundaries of zones subject to variable backwater influence under conditions of maximum and minimum annual reservoir water–level fluctuations

Long-term Earth observation of inland waters depends on continuity between satellite missions, adequate combinations of spectral, spatial and temporal resolution, and representative calibration and validation datasets. Discontinuities and trade-offs in these components constrain the records available for studying inland waters and their change. We examine three gaps affecting inland water remote sensing: a mission gap between comparable 300 m ocean colour observations from MERIS and OLCI during 2012–2016, a coverage gap in spectral, spatial and temporal sampling, and a generalisation gap when retrieval algorithm accuracy declines beyond bio-optical properties and atmospheric conditions represented during development. Foundation models (FMs) could help address these gaps by learning reusable representations from satellite archives before adaptation to a particular retrieval task. We hypothesise that relationships learned across overlapping satellite missions can support reconstruction of what a sensor would have measured during the mission gap, that combining complementary sensors can extend usable observation coverage, and that pretraining on satellite archives, which cover more water bodies and a wider range of bio-optical properties and atmospheric conditions than available field datasets, can improve retrieval algorithm generalisation. Testing these hypotheses requires criteria that define progress. We quantify the three gaps, define a progress criterion for each and assess 100 recent machine learning studies against the criteria. For the mission gap, three studies address continuity across sensor eras, and none recovers a record from a withheld mission period. For the coverage gap, 23 studies combine complementary observations, but only three test them on withheld water bodies or periods. For the generalisation gap, only seven studies withhold whole water bodies or later periods from all model development. Across all three gaps, none of the six studies that use pretraining compares it with the same architecture trained without pretraining on independent water bodies. The assumption common to all three hypotheses, that archive pretraining adds information beyond established methods, therefore remains untested. Applying the criteria to existing generic Earth observation FMs, then to FMs pretrained on inland waters, would determine which gaps pretraining can reduce.

Global-warming-induced shifts in precipitation regimes profoundly affect terrestrial vegetation productivity; however, the pathways through which precipitation characteristics regulate gross primary productivity (GPP) remain insufficiently understood. Using meteorological records, satellite remote-sensing products, and reanalysis data from 2000 to 2024, we quantified GPP responses to changing precipitation regimes in Central Asian drylands through superposed epoch analysis, random forest and TreeSHAP analyses, and cross-lagged structural equation modeling (CB-SEM). Against a background of increasing annual precipitation (1.79 mm yr−1, p = 0.014), synchronous increases in precipitation frequency and intensity enhanced dryland productivity, with increasing GPP (0.28 g C m−2 yr−1, p = 0.726). The two precipitation-frequency metrics increased across 75.10–82.46% of the study area, whereas the intensity metrics increased across 64.16–81.67%. Frequent precipitation rapidly reduced vapor pressure deficit (VPD) and maintained shallow soil moisture, producing GPP anomaly gains ~0.5 g C m−2 8 d−1 across extensive Central Asian plains. In contrast, high-intensity precipitation replenished deep soil moisture and sustained GPP anomaly gains of 0.5–1.5 g C m−2 8 d−1 in the semi-arid steppe of northern Kazakhstan. CB-SEM identified VPD as the strongest direct climatic driver of GPP (−0.482), followed by soil moisture (0.290) and temperature (0.283). Precipitation frequency directly reduced VPD (−0.016), whereas precipitation intensity positively affected soil moisture (0.057). The frequency-mediated atmospheric pathway was strongest during the initial t (0–8-day) response period, while the intensity-mediated soil-moisture pathway became increasingly important after 8 days. These findings reveal complementary atmospheric-regulation and soil-moisture-buffering mechanisms and provide a process-based framework for improving the representation of dryland carbon–water coupling under changing precipitation regimes.

Landscape dynamics are the “big picture” of changes in the growing season, vegetation, and surface water. The length and warmth of the growing season control the amount of plant matter, which is the energy supply for all other biological processes and crucial for wildlife. Major changes in vegetation are likely to benefit some species and harm others. A long-term increase in shrubs in the arctic has already been observed. Formation and drainage of ponds and lakes, which are important habitat for many species, are natural processes that may be accelerated by climate change. Remote sensing provides valuable tools for monitoring landscape patterns and dynamics. Our long-term monitoring program includes 4 different projects that utilize remote sensing to follow landscape change: Analysis of trends in surface greenness as measured from satellites. Satellites have been measuring the amount of sunlight refl ected from the earth in different wavelengths (colors) for over 20 years. We can compute an index of the earth’s greenness from these measurements and determine the length of the growing season and its peak greenness. Analysis of trends in greenness and snow cover measured by remote automated cameras at weather stations. These photographs provide a close-up view of changes in the seasons that can be linked directly to weather data. Analyze changes in vegetation and other land surface features visible on high-resolution aerial photographs. We have a set of detailed aerial photographs taken on a 20-km grid across the Arctic Network. On these photographs we can measure things like shrub cover, tree cover, and area of small ponds caused by thawing permafrost. We plan to repeat these photographs every 10 years and compare the dates to get a networkwide view of changes over time. Analyze the change in area of lakes and ponds using satellite images. Water levels in lakes and ponds in permafrost regions can change rapidly and lakes often drain entirely. These changes can be tracked using inexpensive moderate-resolution satellite imagery. Citation: Miller C. Monitoring Terrestrial Landscape Patterns and Dynamics in the NPS Arctic Network of National Parklands. 2011. National Park Service Leads: Celia Miller (National Park Service) Sponsors: National Park Service Arctic Network Inventory and Monitoring Program Publisher: National Park Service

Environmentally sensitive coastal areas are rapidly becoming urbanised, increasing pressure on vegetation, wetlands, surface-water resources and the natural resource base. The current study combines remote sensing, Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and machine learning to evaluate changes in Land Use/Land Cover (LULC) and environmental conditions in the Lekki–Ajah axis of Lagos State, Nigeria. Built-up areas, vegetation, wetlands, surface water and bare/exposed land were mapped using multitemporal satellite imagery and spatial datasets. Random Forest, Support Vector Machine and Extreme Gradient Boosting algorithms were used to evaluate their performance in land-cover classification, while GIS-based spatial analysis was used to map temporal changes and environmentally sensitive areas. The Random Forest model achieved an overall accuracy of 92%, indicating good performance in discriminating the major land-cover categories within the study environment. The results show substantial urban growth and continued shrinkage of natural and semi-natural vegetation. Historical evidence for Eti-Osa shows that built-up land increased from 2.94% in 1984 to 43.34% in 2002 and 68.38% in 2014, while vegetation declined from 65.53% to 36.87% and 14.86%, respectively. Mangrove cover also declined from 15.21% to 5.04% and 2.98%, respectively, over the same period. Total built-up land cover in the broader Lekki Peninsula rose from 0.44% to 17.98%, while vegetation cover fell from 68.62% to 55.07% between 1984 and 2014. Recent data also show ongoing urbanisation, with an increase in urbanised land from 5.36% in 2002 to 42.37% in 2022, and approximately 49 km of coastline reported as being affected by coastal retreat. The results demonstrate the potential of remote sensing, GIS and machine learning as effective tools for monitoring the rapidly changing Lekki–Ajah coastal area. Increasing developed surfaces and declining vegetation and coastal ecosystems emphasise the need for ongoing geospatial monitoring, protection of remaining wetlands and vegetation resources, environmentally sensitive development planning, and improved coastal-resource management. The study provides a spatial basis for supporting sustainable urban and environmental planning in the rapidly growing Lekki–Ajah corridor.

The growing adoption of digital technologies in agriculture is opening new opportunities for improving productivity, sustainability and resource efficiency through data-driven decision making. This paper presents the integrated precision-agriculture framework developed by RFSAT Limited within the H2020 AgriBIT project and currently being further enhanced through the ENACT project. The framework combines Internet-of-Things (IoT) sensing, centimetre-accuracy Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) positioning, high-resolution multispectral remote sensing and Artificial Intelligence (AI) analytics into a single smart-farming solution. A key enabler is a low-cost, centimetre-accurate GNSS receiver developed by RFSAT, which allows precise georeferencing of aerial and ground observations and, in turn, the generation of high-resolution multispectral 3D models of crop canopies with spatial resolution exceeding 1 cm/pixel. These digital representations support detailed monitoring of crop growth, canopy development, biomass distribution and plant health throughout the season. Fused with an IoT monitoring infrastructure of environmental and microclimatic sensors, the georeferenced remote-sensing products form a comprehensive digital twin of the agricultural environment, over which machine-learning techniques automatically identify and localise crop anomalies including water stress, nutrient deficiencies, disease outbreaks and pest infestations. The technologies have been validated at operational pilot sites across Greece, Portugal and Italy, spanning orchards, vineyards and other high-value crops, where the combination of centimetre positioning, multispectral 3D modelling, IoT monitoring and AI analytics substantially improved monitoring accuracy, reduced input consumption and enhanced management decisions.

Freshwater regulates stratification in marine systems, a key driver of circulation, productivity, and exchange processes. This is especially important in the Arctic Ocean, where nearly one fifth of global freshwater drains, and an intensifying hydrological cycle increases freshwater input. However, Hudson Bay, an Arctic marginal sea that receives three times as much river runoff yield per unit area as the Arctic Ocean, remains one of the least observed components of the Arctic freshwater system. This thesis therefore develops satellite based approaches, supported by field data, to map seasonal distributions of river water (RW) and sea ice melt (SIM), the main freshwater sources in the Hudson Bay marine system. The third chapter examined the dispersion of the combined Nelson and Hayes River plume into southwestern Hudson Bay using satellite-derived chromophoric dissolved organic matter (CDOM) and total suspended solids (TSS). A new method showed that quantile concentrations of CDOM declined exponentially from the river mouth and varied with river discharge, whereas TSS did not, demonstrating CDOM as an effective river plume tracer. Wind forcing further regulated plume transport, with anticyclonic winds driving riverine CDOM towards central Hudson Bay and cyclonic winds promoting eastward alongshore transport. The fourth chapter used satellite-derived salinity and CDOM to map RW and SIM fractions in the surface waters of Hudson Bay and James Bay (HJB), based on RW, SIM, and seawater (SW) fractions derived from salinity–oxygen isotope ratios. Satellite retrievals reproduced known freshwater patterns, with RW dominating southern and eastern regions, particularly in James Bay, which receives the largest riverine inputs within the Hudson Bay marine system. Satellite retrieved SIM prevailed in central Hudson Bay and declined through summer. From 2011 to 2019, RW fractions increased while SIM fractions declined across HJB. Since RW and SIM are evolving in the surface waters of HJB, the fifth chapter determined which freshwater type controls stratification by analyzing salinity, temperature, and oxygen-isotope profiles. Results show that RW dominates stratification year-round, from coastal waters to northern HJB. Projected increases in wintertime RW discharge will likely enhance stratification and may impede deep-water renewal. Therefore, by combining satellite-based ocean color data, salinity, and isotope-based analyses, this thesis advances understanding of freshwater distribution, and stratification in the understudied Hudson Bay marine system.

The combination of geographic information systems (GIS) and remote sensing (RS) technologies has transformed aquaculture and fisheries by providing sophisticated tools for resource management, spatial analysis, and decision-making. Aquatic ecosystems can be mapped and analyzed using GIS, making it easier to identify suitable aquaculture sites, monitor fish habitats, and assess environmental changes. RS, through satellite imagery and aerial photography, provides real-time data on water quality parameters, temperature, chlorophyll concentration, habitat conditions, and coastal land-use changes, which are crucial for sustainable fisheries management. Together, GIS and RS support the prediction and management of fishery resources by analyzing oceanic and freshwater conditions, forecasting potential fishing zones (PFZ), and assessing the impacts of climate change. These technologies also help mitigate risks in aquaculture, such as disease outbreaks and pollution, by enabling early detection and monitoring. 120 Furthermore, they contribute to policy formulation and enforcement by providing reliable data for spatial planning and regulatory compliance. The application of GIS and RS in fisheries and aquaculture not only enhances productivity but also ensures environmental sustainability and resource conservation. This multidisciplinary approach underscores the importance of technological advancements in addressing the challenges of global food security and the sustainable management of aquatic ecosystems.

California agriculture faces escalating water-management challenges from drought and heat while adapting to groundwater-sustainability policies. Accurate field-scale evapotranspiration (ET) values are essential for irrigation decisions and water conservation. OpenET integrates six satellite-based ET models in Google Earth Engine to provide near–real-time actual ET (ET a ) at 30 m and daily resolution. We evaluated OpenET against eddy-covariance ET a from 11 wine-grape vineyards monitored by the Grape Remote sensing Atmospheric Profile & Evapotranspiration eXperiment (GRAPEX). We compared individual-model and ensemble ET a to tower ET a and conducted site-focused analyses to diagnose performance under key microclimate and management conditions. The OpenET ensemble ET a value closely matched tower ET a (daily R 2 = 0.82; MAE = 0.63 mm d -1 ; monthly R 2 = 0.89; MAE = 14.8 mm month -1 ) with negligible bias and generally outperformed individual models. Performance improved with temporal aggregation, consistent with reduced sensitivity to Landsat overpass timing and reference ET-based interpolation at the daily timestep. Skill was highest at monthly and seasonal scales, while daily errors increased during advective conditions and short-lived irrigation deficits, and tower energy-balance closure influenced inferred bias at advection-prone sites. Controlled experiments showed that thermal-based models detected imposed vine water-stress responses directionally (but were dampened in the ensemble) and that winter cover crops, and vine-row orientation produced consistent ET a shifts that propagated into thermal-based OpenET values. These results quantify when OpenET is most reliable for precision viticulture and provide guidance for using satellite ET a to support irrigation scheduling and water accounting in practice.

Marine ecosystems, which are changing due to climate interaction along the coastlines, are also changing ocean-colour properties by altering the phytoplankton communities, suspended solids, dissolved organic matter, and water optical properties. These changes should be monitored continuously to comprehend the response of the ecosystem and sustainability of coastal management. The traditional ocean-colour works mostly depend on either the satellite sensors or field samples which usually lack spatial power, time basing or a direct connection to pigments of phytoplankton. This paper suggests a hyperspectral attribution model combining unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) hyperspectral imagery, which sources multi spectral satellite data, and in situ phytoplankton pigmentation to describe climate-induced shifts in ocean-colour. It is a combination of radiometric preprocessing, atmospheric correction, hyperspectral ocean-colour retrieval, and multi-source data fusion to determine some of the most important optical parameters, such as remote sensing reflectance, water-leaving reflectance, chlorophyll-a concentration, turbidity, colored dissolved organic matter and total suspended matter. Comparison of observation platforms indicates that the retrieval is consistent and enhances describing the spatial and temporal variance in coastal waters. The integrated approach is that high-resolution UAV observations combined with extensive satellite cover complements the identification of the small changes in ocean-colour indicators of climate variability and minimises the uncertainties inherent in individual-platform observations. correlations between recalled optical properties on the one hand and phytoplankton pigments distributions on the other also enhance the explanation of ecological responses to new environmental conditions. Altogether, the suggested framework offers an integrated climate attribution strategy of coastal ocean-colour dynamics along with a useful instrument of long-term ecosystem monitoring, water-quality evaluation as well as evidence-based coastal environmental management in changing climatic conditions.

Coastal wetlands provide essential habitats for migratory waterbirds. Although wetland restoration is increasingly implemented, its effectiveness in improving habitat quality and the ecological mechanisms underlying such improvements remain insufficiently understood. Focusing on Jiangsu Yancheng Wetlands & Rare Birds National Natural Reserve, a key site along the East Asian-Australasian Flyway, this study evaluated whether and how restoration enhanced wintering habitat quality for the endangered Red-crowned Crane ( Grus japonensis ). Using long-term satellite observations, crane occurrence records and restoration project data, we developed an integrated indicator framework characterizing vegetation-water-soil conditions, spatial structure, and temporal hydrological variability. These indicators, together with conventional environmental variables, were combined with MaxEnt habitat modelling and explainable machine learning (XGBoost-SHAP and GAM) to quantify restoration effectiveness, identify environmental drivers, and determine ecological thresholds. Results show the remote sensing indicator framework explained approximately 40% of the spatial variation in crane occurrence, with newly-developed temporal hydrological and spatial metrics increasing explanatory power by 6–10%. Following restoration, highly suitable habitats expanded by 65.1%. Restoration measures including hydrological regulation, pond-to-wetland restoration, and composite restoration produced the largest relative gains in suitable habitat area, increasing it by 34.6%, 128.7%, and 436.8%, respectively. Restoration enhanced habitat quality by increasing seasonal hydrological variability and habitat spatial heterogeneity, creating shallow-water and low-coverage vegetation mosaics, and shifting ecological thresholds toward conditions more favorable for cranes. These findings show that effective restoration depends not only on expanding wetland area but also on re-establishing hydrological dynamics and spatial structure. The framework supports quantitative restoration assessment, evidence-based planning, and adaptive management for coastal wetland sustainability.

This project is a systematic review of how remote sensing is used to monitor the environment in and around mines, and of the accuracy and validation figures that the studies report. Mining changes land cover, soil, water, vegetation and the ground surface. Field surveys are accurate but costly and cover little ground, so satellite, aerial, drone, LiDAR, hyperspectral and radar data are widely used instead. Earlier reviews do not tabulate the numerical accuracy measures that studies report, by platform, outcome and mining type. This review maps that evidence and shows where it is thin. We searched SciSpace, Google Scholar, PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science on 1 October 2026. After de-duplication, 4,457 records were screened and 562 studies were included. Each had to concern a mining area, use remote sensing as a main method, assess an environmental outcome (including land subsidence) and report a numerical accuracy or validation measure. We describe platforms, outcomes, methods, mining types and countries, and report accuracy figures without pooling them. Expected outcomes are a published review in a journal, an evidence map, recommendations for reporting reference data, validation design and sample size, and a base for a later comparison of remote sensing with field monitoring. The review is provisional. Screening and coding were assisted by AI tools and done by one reviewer, the keyword coding has not been checked by hand, and no protocol was registered before the searches. This OSF registration is retrospective, made after screening was complete.

Although intertidal-zone delineation and shoreline or coastal geomorphological classification have been extensively investigated, relatively few studies have integrated these complementary information layers within a unified and operational remote-sensing framework for oil-spill emergency response. With increasing development and marine transportation activities in the Arctic, detailed and spatially explicit shoreline information is essential for oil-spill response planning and coastal hazard assessment along the Canadian Arctic coast. A key challenge is to reliably characterize the spatial extent and geomorphological variability of Arctic intertidal shorelines under substantial temporal variability in tidal inundation and environmental conditions. This study presents a hierarchical shoreline classification framework designed to support oil-spill emergency preparedness and response planning. The framework integrates Sentinel-1 synthetic aperture radar (SAR) backscatter, temporal-change and structural descriptors, and Sentinel-2 water-sensitive indices to derive a composite shore-zone proxy that captures spatial and temporal information on tidal inundation and coastal surface characteristics. This proxy supports Level 1 shore-zone mapping, while high-resolution optical imagery enables subsequent Level 2 shoreline-type classification. The framework was evaluated in four Canadian Arctic coastal areas representing diverse coastal landscapes and environmental conditions, including differences in tidal regimes, water turbidity, floating ice, and geomorphology. Results indicated that mapping accuracy remains constrained for tidal zones and substrates smaller than or comparable to the sensor’s spatial resolution. For Level 1 shore-zone mapping, unsupervised classification of the temporal and composite indices achieved overall mapping accuracies of 56–73% for the Upper Shore Zone across three study areas. For Level 2 shoreline-type mapping, Random Forest classification of high-resolution satellite imagery, including WorldView and GeoEye imagery, achieved overall accuracies of 81–85% across the four study areas. These results demonstrate the potential of the composite shore-zone proxy to integrate complementary SAR and optical information for consistent characterization of Arctic shore zones, while the subsequent shoreline-type classification provides additional geomorphological detail. Together, the hierarchical products provide spatially explicit shoreline information that can support the identification and prioritization of shoreline areas for oil-spill response planning and resource allocation.

Analyzing ocean dynamics from satellite altimetry is one of the most important areas in the field of geodesy. The recent Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission has made it possible to probe fine-scale ocean dynamics using radar remote sensing that measures Sea Surface Height (SSH) and its anomalies (SSHA), the latter being of fundamental importance in analyzing the short-term ocean variations. However, due to the spatiotemporal heterogeneity and sampling irregularity of SSHA data, analyzing SWOT-based ocean dynamics is faced with a multitude of pitfalls. Here we propose a machine learning-based solution to this problem using a framework based upon probabilistic Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Our novel, uncertainty-aware methodology—called SeaWOT—models SSHA and its uncertainty on a global scale using GANs and subsequently predicts them on seasonal timescales (∼90 days ahead). Using gridded SSHA data over the period March 2023 to March 2026, we show that modeling and prediction can be done with an accuracy of ∼0.89 (in terms of coefficient of determination, R-squared, calculated over all grid cells), implying that SeaWOT can accurately capture short-period (seasonal to interannual) dynamics of global oceans. Furthermore, we assess the temporal variations in ocean dynamics by comparing with independent observations from a global network of tide gauges (539 stations), demonstrating the agreement between these independent measurements of up to ∼0.8 (R-squared). Together, these results show that SeaWOT can be a valuable tool for modeling and prediction of ocean dynamics, with application in many different fields, from geodesy and geophysics to ocean science.

Remote sensing can monitor water quality at a large scale and low cost, but many existing models are narrowly tuned and hard to generalize. To the best of our knowledge, this study introduces a reproducible, end-to-end evaluation framework for Landsat-based water quality modeling. It compares machine learning algorithms, water quality indicators, cloud-cover thresholds, temporal matching windows, and water body types using a single standardized dataset. Using AquaSat, with over 600,000 matched in situ and Landsat observations, we evaluated 27,720 model configurations across eleven algorithms, six indicators, seven cloud-cover thresholds, five water body types, and temporal offsets up to ± 48 h, under one harmonized hyperparameter configuration on the Landsat 5, 7, and 8 family. Every configuration was evaluated twice: under a random splitting protocol and 50 km spatially blocked validation. Under the random protocol, 95.8% of the held-out observations came from sampling sites also represented in the training data, while under spatial blocking, no sampling site was shared between the training and test sets. The median r 2 decreased by 0.087 between the two. Three of the six indicators retain meaningful skill under blocked validation: the best models for total inorganic sediment, Secchi depth, and dissolved organic carbon average an r 2 of 0.403, while chlorophyll-a and percent sand showed little or no predictive skill. These results indicate that poor blocked-validation performance primarily reflects limited spatial transfer rather than failure to fit the training data: 98.7% of the configurations with a negative held-out r 2 fitted their training data successfully, and a hyperparameter search across 15,578 paired comparisons, pooled over both splitting schemes, moved held-out performance by −0.001.
