Radial growth in seasonally dry tropical forests is an important indicator of the relationships among climate, water availability, and cambial activity.This study evaluated the relationships between satellite remote-sensing variables and the treering width (TRW) of Cedrela odorata L. (Cedro) in a seasonally dry tropical forest in the municipality of Lagarto, Sergipe, Brazil.Tree-ring measurements provided the dendrochronological data.The explanatory variables comprised spectral metrics derived from Landsat imagery, including NDVI, EVI2, SAVI, GV, NPV, and the seasonal amplitudes of these indices, as well as annual precipitation data from CHIRPS and ERA5.Correlation analyses were first conducted between TRW and the environmental variables, followed by an exploratory random forest assessment of the relative importance of the explanatory variables.The results showed that spectral indices and, to a lesser extent, precipitation variables were significantly correlated with the TRW of Cedrela odorata L. in the study area.These findings indicate that the species' TRW is closely associated with water availability and the functional state of the vegetation.Annual precipitation data and spectral metrics at medium and coarse spatial resolutions may therefore help explain TRW responses to water availability, highlighting the potential of remote sensing as a complementary tool to dendrochronology in ecological and forest-monitoring studies.

This dataset originates from tower-based noncontact hyperspectral remote sensing observations of the natural water surface of Poyang Lake during 2020–2021. Observations were acquired with a QE65Pro spectrometer (spectral range 650–800 nm, spectral resolution approximately 0.3 nm FWHM, nominal sampling interval approximately 3 min). Observation dates were screened using camera records, and only dates with complete water-surface inundation were retained. Raw spectra underwent upstream retrieval and sequential quality control: starting from 11,188 matched observations, the chain applied a 650–800 nm spectral-validity screen, a solar zenith angle ≤80° screen, local PAR anomaly (3σ) and suspected sun-glint screens, and a finite-positive-value screen, leaving 4,881 retained observations at approximately 3-min intervals. The released aggregated products are fixed nonoverlapping 30-min and daily arithmetic means without interpolation. Data fields include red SIF (retrieved by the 3FLD method, SIF_3FLD, with iFLD and SFM diagnostic retrievals also provided), the radiance-based fluorescence line height FLH_Rad (mW m⁻² nm⁻¹ sr⁻¹), the remote-sensing-reflectance line height FLH_Ref (obtained by dividing the historical apparent reflectance factor by π, in sr⁻¹), PAR calculated from the 650–790 nm sky spectrum (μmol m⁻² s⁻¹), solar zenith angle (degrees), and various quality-control flags. This is a processed-data-level release; raw spectral files, calibration products, and the upstream retrieval code are not included.The data cover 46 noncontinuous dates during 2020–2021 (not a continuous two-year record); all times are local civil time (UTC+08:00). Spatially, the data correspond to a single fixed tower site at Poyang Lake (point-scale observations; coordinates are given in the associated manuscript). Temporal resolutions are 3 min (native observations) and 30 min/daily (aggregated products). The main table pyh_sif_flh_3min.csv contains 4,881 rows × 39 columns, one row per 3-min observation; pyh_sif_flh_30min_reference.csv contains 708 rows × 20 columns, one row per 30-min mean (the NRawInBin column records the number of contributing observations, ranging from 1 to 13). Row identifiers include Date (YYYYMMDD), Year, and Bin30 (lower edge of the 30-min interval); full field definitions and units are provided in the accompanying data_dictionary.csv. Note that SIF_PAR is the ratio of 30-min means and is not interchangeable with the historical 3-min ratio field aSIF.Missing data: the observation dates are noncontinuous and no interpolation is performed between dates; local-window diagnostic columns are missing near date edges where a complete window is unavailable; 30-min aggregation allows bins with only one observation, and missing dates and bins are not filled; records excluded by quality control are not included, with only per-stage counts provided. Errors and limitations: reflectance-derived fields inherit the upstream sky-reference calibration convention (E_d/π) and were uniformly divided by π for this release (scale factor 0.3183); PAR is a calculated estimate relying on the historical π×1.2 energy-to-photon conversion coefficient; the suspected-glint screen does not prove complete removal of sun glint; the 708 half-hour means arise from a time series and should not be treated as statistically independent; the red SIF–FLH relationship is specific to this site, observation geometry, and instrument processing and requires validation before transfer to other waters, seasons, instruments, or satellite scales.The dataset contains five CSV data files: pyh_sif_flh_3min.csv (main 3-min observation table), pyh_sif_flh_30min_reference.csv (locked 30-min aggregation reference table used to verify the public aggregation implementation), filtering_stats.csv (6 rows; per-stage counts and statistics of the upstream sequential quality control), fig2_spectral_definitions_source.csv (1,021 rows; the single remote-sensing-reflectance spectrum used in manuscript Fig. 2 with window annotations), and fig2_spectral_definitions_metadata.csv (1 row; selection metadata for the Fig. 2 spectrum). Accompanying files include data_dictionary.csv (field dictionary), processing_method.md (processing method), provenance.yaml (provenance), README.md and KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md (usage notes and known limitations), and checksums.sha256 (integrity checksums). All data files are UTF-8 encoded CSV in a general-purpose format readable directly by Excel, WPS, R, Python, and other common software.

Microseira wollei (formerly Lyngbya wollei ) is a problematic benthic cyanobacterium that has proliferated to nuisance densities in western Lake St. Clair, USA. Quantifying the spatial distribution and temporal dynamics of M. wollei is challenging in a large (~1100 km 2 ), dynamic lake system where benthic mats may occur across extensive and heterogeneous nearshore areas. Traditional field surveys are difficult to scale across large ecosystems, creating a need for complementary monitoring technologies. This study evaluated a hybrid framework combining field surveys, autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV), aerial, and satellite imagery to characterize the distribution and monitoring utility of benthic M . wollei . An 80 km 2 region of the western Lake St. Clair shoreline was surveyed using an AUV equipped with a bottom-facing camera, high-resolution aerial imagery (4.4–7 cm pixel −1 ), and WorldView-2 multispectral imagery. AUV imagery successfully discriminated M . wollei from mixed submerged aquatic vegetation and benthic algal assemblages from the shoreline to approximately 2.2 km offshore. High-resolution aerial imagery distinguished benthic assemblages within 900 m of the shoreline (≤ 1 m water depth) and quantified relative changes in percent cover over a 10 year period. WorldView-2 image assessment provided regional spatial context for nearshore benthic assemblages under favorable optical conditions but was constrained by turbidity, water-column effects, and atmospheric correction uncertainties. Collectively, these complementary technologies provide a scalable monitoring framework that supports detection, field verification, temporal monitoring, and adaptive management of benthic harmful algal blooms in large freshwater ecosystems.

Shoreline analysis is an important aspect of coastal studies, as coastlines are continuously influenced by natural processes such as waves, tides, currents, and human activities. Monitoring these changes is essential for effective coastal management, environmental protection and sustainable development. This research work focuses on the analysis of shoreline characteristics along the Machilipatnam coast in Krishna District, Andhra Pradesh, using geospatial techniques. Landsat ETM + satellite imagery for the period 2018 to 2022 was used as the primary data source. The satellite data provides multispectral information with moderate spatial resolution, making it suitable for coastal analysis. The images were processed using QGIS software, where band combination and colour composite techniques were applied to enhance the visual distinction between land and water features. A layer stack approach was used to organize raster data for better interpretation. The shoreline was identified based on textural variations and digitized as a vector line layer. Additionally, the land and water regions were digitized as polygon layers to enable spatial analysis. Various GIS tools were used to calculate shoreline length and area measurements, allowing for systematic comparison across multiple years. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of integrating remote sensing and GIS techniques for shoreline mapping and analysis.

Remote sensing provides critical insights into reservoir operations at sites with minimal in-situ data. The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission improves upon previous satellite altimetry missions with two-dimensional water surface representations, enhanced discharge estimates, and simultaneous water surface elevation (WSE) and surface area/width data. We found median agreement (Spearman rho) greater than 0.9 between SWOT and 773 United States Geological Survey (USGS; ρ = 0.96) and US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE; ρ = 0.94) WSE time series at Conterminous US reservoirs. At USGS sites, 68% of observations had relative errors compared to in-situ observations (after adjusting for bias using time series average WSE) with an absolute value under 10 cm, versus 22 cm at USACE sites. However, low agreement clusters appeared in the Pacific Northwest and Southeastern US. For SWOT-derived downstream discharge, agreement (ρ) with in-situ data was lower (USACE: 0.57, USGS: 0.39) with a low performance cluster in the Pacific Northwest and a high performance cluster in the central US. At USGS sites, 68% of observations had relative errors with an absolute value under 108 cubic meters per second (m 3 /s), compared to 133 m 3 /s at USACE sites. This research supports the ability of SWOT to accurately represent reservoir water levels at ungauged sites while recognizing potential for improvement on downstream discharge estimates.

The present study was conducted to assess the changes in the Zionist Entity settlement patterns in West Bank, Palestine, between 2011 and 2026. The study focused on the changes that happened to agricultural lands. The research used the remote sensing method to analyze the data and evaluate the tendencies in the spread of settlements in the selected area. The authors used satellite images and geographic information systems (GIS) to observe the growth of the Zionist Entity settlements, recognize the new developed areas, and study the changes in the land cover. The study aimed to analyze built-up regions, agricultural land, vegetation, barren land, and water resources. It also intended to identify hotspot settlements, compare the selected clusters, observe the changes in roads, and investigate the alterations in land use within the region. The authors used a combination of image classification, change detection, overlay, and hotspot analysis methods to address the objectives of the study. The main purpose of the study was to create a basis for understanding the spread of settlements and better observe the changes related to agriculture and the nearby localities using remote sensing and GIS technology.

Flood is one of the most important hydro-meteorological hazards affecting human settlements, agriculture, infrastructure and regional economies. Chitrakoot district of Uttar Pradesh presents a distinctive case of hydro-climatic vulnerability because it belongs to the drought-prone Bundelkhand region but simultaneously experiences recurrent riverine and flash-flood conditions during intense monsoon rainfall. The present study assesses the spatial characteristics and determinants of flood hazard and vulnerability in Chitrakoot district using an integrated geographical, GIS and remote sensing approach. The analysis incorporates the Digital Elevation Model (DEM), drainage network, physiography, river proximity, historical flood information, satellite-based flood observations and socio-economic exposure. The district's DEM indicates a marked elevation gradient, approximately from 66 m to 451 m, with relatively higher terrain in the southern part and lower terrain towards the northern Yamuna valley. This topographic configuration facilitates rapid surface runoff from elevated southern terrain towards comparatively low-lying riverine areas. The drainage system is dominated by the Yamuna and Mandakini/Paisuni systems along with Baghain, Gunta, Bardaha and smaller tributaries. The Uttar Pradesh Flood Hazard Atlas identifies 5,114 ha of flood-hazard area in Chitrakoot for 1998–2020, of which 4,129 ha (81%) falls in the very-low hazard category and 985 ha (19%) in the low-hazard category. However, the historical classification does not fully represent the potential consequences of extreme rainfall events. The August 2026 flood provides compelling evidence: the Mandakini at Chitrakoot reached a reported new high flood level of 145.60 m on 29 August 2026, approximately 2.95 m above the previous reported high level, while the water level rose by about 7.5 m within six hours. The study concludes that flood risk in Chitrakoot is spatially concentrated around river corridors, low-elevation areas, floodplains, agricultural land, settlements and tourism infrastructure. A shift from conventional relief-oriented flood management towards integrated floodplain regulation, watershed management, GIS-based risk zonation, real-time monitoring and community-based preparedness is therefore essential.

This study presents a planning-oriented high-resolution land cover dataset for China, developed to address the limitations of existing products in territorial spatial planning and regional land analysis. The dataset integrates 2-m optical satellite imagery with official planning maps using a deep learning semantic segmentation framework based on ConvNeXt. It includes six land cover classes—built-up areas, cropland, roads, green spaces, water bodies, and others—and is designed to better align remote-sensing outputs with planning-relevant land categories. We conducted a comprehensive validation using pixel-level test-set evaluation, point-based assessment with an open-access validation dataset, and nationwide areal consistency analysis against aggregated results from China’s Third National Land Survey. The product achieved competitive classification performance and showed the strongest agreement with official area statistics among the compared datasets, particularly for built-up areas, cropland, and roads. Visual comparisons further demonstrate clearer boundary delineation and more realistic spatial patterns in both urban and rural settings. As a planning-oriented baseline dataset, this product is particularly useful for built-up land accounting, cropland protection assessment, urban–rural spatial analysis, road-network extraction, and regional policy evaluation in situations where up-to-date survey data are unavailable. Its combination of high spatial resolution, strong semantic consistency, and nationwide coverage makes it valuable for both research and practical decision-making in China’s territorial spatial planning.

Thanks to advancements in technology, satellite remote sensing provides a valuable means of monitoring the spatial and temporal responses of vegetation, surface moisture conditions, and land surface temperature to drought. Its capacity to monitor large areas with high temporal continuity significantly eliminates the spatial limitations of ground observations. This allows for the simultaneous and comparable analysis of key variables such as vegetation dynamics, soil moisture, and land surface temperature. Indicators such as the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Normalized Difference Moisture Index (NDMI), and Land Surface Temperature (LST) provide complementary information on vegetation condition, surface moisture, and thermal stress, thereby supporting drought monitoring. This integrated monitoring framework supports the sustainable management of water resources while strengthening the scientific basis of decision-making processes, significantly contributing to disaster risk reduction. This study comparatively evaluates NDVI, NDMI, and LST values derived from Landsat 8 data obtained in March, April, and May between 2019 and 2022, and examines the relationships between these variables across the Northern Aegean Drainage Basin (NADB). The results show increasingly strong negative relationships between LST and the spectral indices from March to May, with the strongest correlations observed in May for NDMI–LST (r = −0.78) and NDVI–LST (r = −0.74). The NDMI-LST relationship can be said to be slightly better than the NDVI-LST relationship. The correlation coefficient between NDMI and NDVI was calculated to be lowest in March at r=0.54 and highest in May at r=0.90. It was determined that areas with high LST values had lower NDVI and NDMI values. Drought monitoring using remote sensing methods is important in terms of time and accuracy, but it is not sufficient on its own. In addition to problems arising from satellite imagery, land surfaces are affected by short-term climatic factors. Therefore, the indices obtained from satellite images must be evaluated together with meteorological and terrestrial data. However, it is thought that satellite-based drought monitoring will produce more reliable results under current technological and methodological conditions.

Land Use/Land Cover (LU/LC) serve as essential indicators of global environmental changes. This study examined the LU/LC change in the East Medinipur district of West Bengal, India, using remote sensing data and the CA-Markov modeling approach. Through GIS tools and satellite imagery, the study maps, monitors, and analyzes LU/LC changes over a 20-year period (2001–2021), utilizing data from Landsat 4–5 and Landsat 8. Analytical tools including ArcGIS 9, IDRISI Terset, and ERDAS 2014 are employed to project LU/LC trends up to 2041. The results highlight significant transformations, notable reductions in agriculture, vegetation, barren land, and water bodies, alongside substantial increases in aquaculture and built-up areas from 2001 to 2021. Projections indicates that these trends will continue through 2041, with further declines in agriculture, vegetation, barren land, and water bodies, accompanied by continued growth in aquaculture and built-up areas.

Satellite remote sensing offers a scalable solution for water quality monitoring in small to medium sized lakes, yet whether current methods capture seasonal dynamics and long-term trends accurately remains untested. We developed LakeSense, an automated pipeline retrieving water quality time series (WQTS) from Sentinel-2A/B Multispectral Imager (MSI) and Landsat-8/9 Operational Land Imager (OLI), and evaluated how sensor, atmospheric correction (AC), and algorithm choice affect chlorophyll a , turbidity, and Secchi depth accuracy. Across 102 diverse U.S. lakes, we matched in situ observations to overpasses (±3 days) corrected with three aquatic AC (DSF, RAdCor, GAAC) and two non-aquatic Level-2 products (Sen2Cor, LaSRC). Quality control retained 14-21 % of Sentinel-2A/B and 19-31 % of Landsat-8/9 matchups, varying by AC. The Mishra Normalized Difference Chlorophyll Index on RAdCor-corrected Sentinel-2A/B performed best for chlorophyll a (R 2 = 0.64); machine-learning models on DSF-corrected imagery performed best for turbidity (R 2 = 0.67) and Secchi depth (R 2 = 0.70). Aquatic AC marginally yet consistently outperformed non-aquatic AC: DSF and RAdCor tracked in situ variability most closely, whereas GAAC achieved the lowest bias. Sentinel-2A/B outperformed Landsat-8/9, largely due to red-edge bands and finer spatial and temporal resolution. Time series generated from best methods resolved seasonal and long-term dynamics, and the aquatic versus non-aquatic AC accuracy gap narrowed for multi-year trends as retrieval uncertainty became proportionally less influential. Findings indicate that satellite remote sensing can produce reliable WQTS across diverse lakes, though retrievals would benefit from regionally calibrated algorithms and upcoming sensors with higher spectral resolution.

Comparable ecosystem service mapping across international borders requires inputs and choices that remain consistent across the study area. We harmonized satellite-derived and geospatial datasets for the Heilongjiang–Amur River Basin to a common 1 km grid for 2000, 2010, and 2020. Landsat-derived land cover, MODIS burned area, harmonized nighttime lights, terrain, climate, and modeled soil products supported four InVEST indicators: Habitat Quality, Carbon Storage, Annual Water Yield, and Soil Retention. Pooled p01–p99 normalization and equal weighting produced a dimensionless, relative, modeled integrated ES index. Robustness was assessed using alternative normalization, leave-one-service-out tests, bounded weight perturbation, land-cover-excluded XGBoost–SHAP models, and spatially blocked cross-validation. The basin-wide mean index values were 0.444, 0.461, and 0.451. The Chinese-side means were 0.357, 0.365, and 0.361, compared to 0.528, 0.555, and 0.538 on the Russian side; the Russia–China contrast remained positive across tested construction alternatives. The random-split R2 values were 0.819, 0.806, and 0.793, whereas the spatially blocked R2 values were 0.651, 0.582, and 0.606. SHAP analysis characterized associations in fitted predictions rather than causal effects. The three benchmark-year differences are indicative and remain sensitive to Annual Water Yield, interannual climate, and index construction.

Crop breeding depends on characterizing genetic diversity, but phenotyping remains a bottleneck relative to genotyping, motivating interest in hyperspectral imaging, which captures continuous reflectance curves shaped by leaf pigments, water, nitrogen and structure, together forming a "spectral phenotype." Genotype-oriented spectral libraries linking this spectral phenotype rigorously to genetic diversity remain scarce, and remote sensing and genetics literatures have developed largely in isolation. This review addresses that gap by synthesizing evidence on the biological pathway from genotype to spectrum, spectral library design and metadata standards, preprocessing and feature-selection methods, machine learning and validation practices, and cross-scale sensing from field to UAV to satellite, drawing on studies across rice, wheat, maize, soybean, cotton and other crops. Findings show genotype and variety discrimination is achievable, particularly at leaf and seed level under controlled conditions, but reported accuracies are frequently confounded by growth stage and genotype-by environment effects and inflated by scan-level data leakage rather than genuine genetic signal. Discriminating wavelengths cluster in red-edge and pigment-sensitive visible regions for canopy studies and extend into shortwave infrared for composition-driven seed studies, while standardized, multi-environment libraries with grouped validation remain rare and genomic integration is concentrated in few groups and crops. A standardized, metadata-rich library framework coupling spectral phenotypes with genomic data could enable cost-effective germplasm screening, genomic prediction and improved breeding decisions, provided rigorous external validation and explicit biological interpretation accompany future work before spectral discrimination is trusted as a genetic proxy.

Lakes are crucial markers of climate fluctuations, yet identifying water bodies in mountainous regions remains a persistent challenge for satellite remote sensing due to terrain-induced obstacles and dynamic surface conditions of ice and snow. We present a novel approach based solely on Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data that allows for the detection of lakes as well as the tracking of their surface area and conditions in mountainous terrain. Our methodology is built around a new index called OASIS, which uses pairs of SAR images to detect and monitor lake surface conditions. We show that this index provides critical insights into lake surface conditions, including the onset and duration of ice cover and the observation of frozen lakes concealed beneath snow. We evaluate this capacity using in situ lake temperature measurements at Arpont Lake. At this lake, the estimated open-water onset typically occurs in mid- to late July, with an ice-free season lasting roughly three to three and a half months. The years 2017 and especially 2022 stand out, showing an earlier break-up (2 July and 24 June, respectively) and longer open-water periods (114 and 132 days; revisit 6 days in 2017–2021 and 12 days in 2016 and 2022–2024). When combined with a segmentation technique, the index allows for accurate quantification and tracking of temporal changes in lake surface area, highlighting lakes that experienced severe drought from 2016 to 2024 in the French Alps. We successfully validated our lake surface area estimates using state-of-the-art lake databases derived from optical sensors.

Rapid urbanization and the associated expansion of built-up areas are transforming land resources, ecosystem functions, and the spatial structure of cities. Distinguishing urban growth, urban expansion, and urban sprawl is essential for understanding the processes and patterns of urban transformation and supporting sustainable urban planning. This study integrates machine learning and geospatial technologies to analyze spatio-temporal land use and land cover (LULC) dynamics and urban expansion in Gambella Town, Ethiopia. Multi-temporal Landsat satellite images from 2005, 2015, and 2025 were processed using remote sensing techniques and a supervised machine learning approach based on the Random Forest (RF) classifier. Six major LULC classes were identified: Agricultural Land, Bush with Grass, Built-Up Area, Bare Land, Forest Land, and Water Bodies. The classification achieved overall accuracies of 90%, 90%, and 89% for 2005, 2015, and 2025, respectively. The results revealed substantial land transformation and rapid physical urban expansion, with the built-up area increasing from 93 ha (2.0%) in 2005–1,956 ha (41.3%) in 2025. This expansion was accompanied by major transformations of surrounding land resources, particularly the conversion of Bush with Grass and other open areas to built-up land. Agricultural land increased from 634 ha (13.4%) to 1,750 ha (36.9%), whereas Bush with Grass declined from 3,375 ha (71.1%) to 652 ha (13.7%). Socio-economic information collected from 277 respondents indicated that population growth, rural–urban migration, housing demand, employment opportunities, and infrastructure development were major drivers of urban expansion. The study distinguishes urban expansion, represented by the increase in built-up land, from urban sprawl, which refers to the spatial pattern and form of outward urban development. The integration of Random Forest classification and GIS-based spatial analysis provides valuable evidence of land transformation, vegetation loss, and increasing pressure on urban services, supporting more sustainable urban planning and land management in Gambella Town.

Water quality degradation, increasing drought severity, and low BMP adoption threaten grazing systems, but riparian protection, adaptive grazing, precision livestock technologies, and coordinated Extension–Natural Resources Conservation Service support can meaningfully improve resilience and water outcomes. Feedyards face parallel challenges, particularly nutrient‑laden runoff, high indirect water use for feed, and declining irrigation supplies, yet innovations in manure management, wastewater reuse, and low‑water forage systems offer viable pathways to reduce water demand. Significant knowledge gaps remain, including limited watershed‑scale data, insufficient evaluation of technologies, and the need for practical reuse strategies and drought‑tolerant feed crops. Long‑term water sustainability requires systems‑level approaches, improved incentives, and policy alignment, as technological efficiency alone cannot overcome economic and operational barriers to widespread adoption. Cattle production is a cornerstone of U.S. agriculture, but it faces growing scrutiny regarding sustainability. A key driver of industry adoption of more sustainable production systems is consumer demand for environmentally responsible food products, along with evolving opportunities for market differentiation (Ishaq et al., 2024). This review evaluates water-related challenges in grazing and feedlot systems, synthesizes current research on watershed impacts and the beef water footprint, and highlights emerging strategies to support more sustainable animal production. It identifies best management practices (BMPs) for enhancing water resources, collaborative strategies for water stewardship, and critical knowledge gaps. By mapping existing studies and identifying priority areas for further investigation, this article aims to draw a cohesive roadmap for scalable interventions to enhance water sustainability in US beef production. The upstream value chain within the domestic beef-production system in the United States features a wide variety of extensive components (Heflin et al., 2019) wherein cattle graze native rangeland, native pastures, and/or modified pasture, thereby taking advantage of the ruminant’s capacity to convert relatively low-digestibility plant materials into animal protein and fat. Those rangelands and pastures may nourish beef cattle at any growth stage, including unweaned and weaned calves, stocker cattle, and even finishing animals, depending on the interaction of market conditions with forage availability and quality. Although well over 90% of the domestic beef slaughter consists of animals that have spent some time in a confinement system (aka “feedyard” or “feedlot”) (ERS, 2025), nearly all such animals have spent a substantial proportion of their lives on some kind of grazing resource. Indeed, beef cattle are grazed throughout the entire United States on resources of highly variable quality and productivity in both space and time, but the contemporary interest in the carbon footprint of domestic beef production has focused attention on the Great Plains ecosystem, where grazing beef cattle have largely displaced native American Bison (Allred et al., 2011; De Bernardi et al., 2025) since the late 1800 s. Challenge: Direct cattle access to surface waterbodies can lead to water quality issues like nutrient loading, pathogen contamination, bank destabilization, erosion, and degradation of riparian and aquatic habitats (Agouridis et al., 2005, Figure 1). Overgrazing of upland areas further exacerbates nutrient, sediment, and bacterial runoff to nearby waterbodies. Bacterial source tracking studies in Texas indicate that cattle and other domestic animals contribute 14–29% of bacterial loading in impaired waterbodies (Di Giovanni et al., 2013). The Oklahoma DEQ identifies “riparian grazing” and “rangeland grazing” as two of the top five sources of lake and river impairment for the state (Phillippe, 2024). These issues have resulted in Total Maximum Daily Loads (including the high profile Chesapeake Bay TMDL in Maryland, Virginia and surrounding states, and Tomales Bay Pathogen TMDL in California) and watershed based plans (including the Lake Okeechobee Basin Management Action Plan in Florida and Lavaca River Watershed Protection Plan in Texas) frequently identifying cattle as major contributors to pollution in the Midwest, West, Rocky Mountains, Southwest, and South, and recommending implementation of grazing and riparian protection BMPs (Agouridis et al., 2005). Cattle with access to streams can cause bank erosion and increase nutrient loading in the waterways. Challenge: Drought has long posed a major challenge to cattle production. Reduced precipitation lowers the quantity and quality of available forage, increases reliance on supplemental feed, diminishes animal condition, and triggers costly destocking–restocking cycles, which elevates operating expenses and reduces overall profitability. Furthermore, soil infiltration and water retention are widely recognized as primary constraints in grazing land ecosystems (Teague et al., 2011). In regions dependent on groundwater, these impacts may be compounded by declining aquifer levels and water scarcity, which can reduce both the availability and quality of water for grazing and feeding operations (Theurer et al., 2026). Historically, U.S. cattle numbers declined during major droughts but recovered by subsequent agricultural censuses. However, the 2010s drought, often viewed as indicative of future extreme drought conditions, resulted in substantial regional cattle inventory declines. Relative to the 2007 census, cattle numbers declined 17.6% in the Southern Plains (Klemm and Briske, 2021). Before cattle numbers rebounded, the 2020 to 2025 drought reduced cattle numbers to their lowest since the 1950s, forcing packing plant shutdowns and reduced shifts. As droughts increase globally, producers are seeking management practices to enhance resilience. Challenge: Limited adoption of improved grazing systems may stem from knowledge gaps or insufficient economic incentives. Forage responses to improved grazing systems often require several years to reach full production potential which delays returns on producer investment and reduces the practices’ near‑term economic appeal (Dyer et al., 2021). Further, improved grazing practice adoption is often limited by the need for additional fencing, increased labor, and reliance on leased land. High fencing costs, the inflexibility of permanent structures, and the difficulty of installing fences in floodplains discourage landowners from implementing measures like riparian protection and rotational grazing systems. As a result, only 25% of cattle operations in the Southern Plains employ rotational grazing systems (Murray et al., 2025). Solution: Practices supporting riparian protection (riparian fencing, off-stream water, shade structures, limited riparian grazing, etc.) have been shown to effectively reduce sediment and fecal bacteria by mitigating riparian vegetation trampling, in-stream defecation, and streambed disturbance from cattle (Grudzinski et al., 2020). Relative to direct stream deposition, manure deposited 0.6 m and 2.1 m from a stream reduced bacterial inputs by 83% and 95%, respectively (Larsen et al., 1994). Targeted grazing of riparian pastures has been proposed as a mitigation strategy, as E. coli concentrations were 88% lower when runoff occurred more than 2 wk after grazing, compared with runoff during or immediately following grazing (Wagner et al., 2012). This suggests that timing riparian grazing with ­periods of low rainfall risk may reduce contamination. Solution: Grazing practices that restore soil function by increasing ground cover and soil carbon have been proposed to enhance drought resilience by improving infiltration and soil water‑holding capacity, thereby accelerating recovery following droughts and pluvial disturbances (Teague and Kreuter, 2020; Dyer et al., 2021). Furthermore, grazing systems that improve manure distribution and vegetative cover can also enhance infiltration, runoff filtration, and water quality when used in conjunction with moderate stocking rates (Briske et al., 2011). Several rotational grazing systems (e.g., adaptive multi‑paddock [AMP], prescriptive, pyric herbivory) have been developed as alternatives to continuous grazing. Empirical and modeling studies indicate reduced runoff and pollutant losses under these systems relative to continuous grazing. Wagner et al. (2023) reported 24% greater edge-of-field runoff and significantly higher nitrogen and sediment losses under continuous grazing compared with prescribed grazing. Ranch‑scale APEX model simulations suggest AMP grazing reduces runoff, sediment, and nutrient losses by 44% to 48% relative to light continuous grazing, and 142% to 158% relative to heavy continuous grazing (Park et al., 2017). Similarly, watershed-scale SWAT modeling showed consistent reductions in hydrologic losses and pollutant export when shifting from heavy continuous to AMP grazing (Park et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2023; Figure 2). Simulated runoff, streamflow, sediment, total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP) reductions from conversion from heavy continuous grazing to AMP in the Apple (North Dakota), Lower Prairie Dog Town Fork (Texas), and Clear Creek (Texas) watersheds. Despite these trends, ecosystem responses to AMP grazing are not uniform. Whereas Hillenbrand et al. (2019) observed significantly higher infiltration under AMP than heavy continuous grazing in South Dakota, Teague et al. (2011) found no treatment differences in infiltration or hydraulic conductivity across four Texas ranches under heavy continuous, light continuous, and AMP grazing. However, runoff measured via rainfall simulator was significantly lower only under light continuous, whereas sediment loss was significantly higher only under heavy continuous. Soil moisture was also significantly lower under heavy continuous compared with all other management treatments (Teague et al., 2011). Collectively, this suggests that while AMP grazing can enhance hydrologic function and water quality, outcomes depend on stocking rate, climate, and site‑specific soil conditions. Solution: Precision livestock technologies provide real-time data, enabling ranchers to take timely action. New technologies like virtual fencing (VF) offer a promising alternative to help address adoption barriers and improve the feasibility of implementing adaptive grazing management by reducing the need for physical fences and the labor demands of manual herd movement. Short-term trials in Oklahoma suggest VF is effective for managing cattle, with cattle compliance with exclusion zones exceeding 80% (Murray et al., 2025). In addition to VF, wearable sensors and tags that track cattle grazing and remote sensing using drones and satellite imagery to monitor forage biomass and quality offer new opportunities to enhance grazing management and sustainability (Marchegiani et al., 2025). Solution: Coordination between Extension educational programming and USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) technical and financial support can strengthen adoption and long‑term effectiveness of BMPs (Peterson et al., 2015). Peterson et al. (2015) examined factors influencing conservation practice adoption among Texas beef cattle producers and identified engagement with Extension services as the strongest predictor of adoption. Similarly, Dewald et al. (2019) found that landowners identified Extension as the most trustworthy source of water related information in Texas. Financial incentives can influence adoption of prescribed grazing, but their effectiveness depends strongly on ecological and economic context. Dyer et al., (2021) showed that producer returns from soil‑health–oriented grazing practices depend on forage response dynamics, initial rangeland condition, implementation costs, and producer discount rates. When delayed productivity gains and establishment costs are considered, substantial incentives are often required to reach break‑even outcomes, particularly for profit‑maximizing ranchers. However, financial incentives alone are insufficient to achieve meaningful conservation outcomes. Briske et al., (2011) reported that structural investments such as fencing or water developments yield limited benefits without effective management, underscoring the importance of managerial capacity. Greater coordination between Extension and the USDA NRCS offers a promising pathway to enhance adoption. Peterson et al. (2015) highlighted the value of integrating NRCS technical and financial support with Extension’s educational infrastructure through long‑term partnerships. Landscape and jurisdictional approaches (LJAs) that bring together stakeholders within a defined geographical area offer the scale needed to address landscape-level processes affecting biodiversity and ecosystem function conservation and restoration in beef-producing regions. LJAs can help overcome traceability barriers by providing a geographical boundary within which both direct and indirect suppliers can be supported to work toward landscape targets. Ecosystem extent and ecosystem condition are two metrics essential for establishing a baseline of biodiversity values within beef-producing landscapes and can play an important role in evaluating the success of LJAs. The provision of robust technical assistance for producers, private and public sector engagement, and the establishment of multistakeholder platforms support the success of LJAs. Beef-production systems play a key role in the intersection between food production, biodiversity conservation, and preservation of ecosystem functions (Gerber et al., 2015). As global interest in the concept of “Nature Positive” increases, in parallel to an increasing world population and demand for protein sources, it will be necessary to ensure that beef-producing landscapes contribute to the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) mission of “halting and reversing” global biodiversity loss (Convention on Biological Diversity, 2022). Achieving this outcome will require efforts to avoid and minimize negative impacts on biodiversity wherever possible and compensating for unavoidable impacts with better-than-equivalent biodiversity gains, facilitated via ecosystem restoration (Maron et al., 2024). In particular, Target 10 of the GBF focuses on enhancing biodiversity and sustainability in agriculture and other production systems. As such, being able to measure, monitor and report on the state of biodiversity and ecosystem functions across beef-producing landscapes that can vary immensely in production systems, environments, climates and governance is essential to underpin the GBF mission and support long-term resilience of production lands. Engagement in sustainability initiatives that seek to improve net environmental outcomes alongside production can offer opportunities for producers, governments and the private sector alike. Governments are taking steps to measure the economic value provided by ecosystems, and their role in national security (Australian Bureau of Statistics, 2026; Department of Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, 2026a). Processors, manufacturers, retailers, and brands are also increasingly interested in the ecological integrity of beef-production systems, as they recognize their business dependencies on ecosystems and look to safeguard future supply, reduce volatility and risks within their supply chains, and support storytelling and communications about partnership within farming communities (Consumer Goods Forum, 2025). As a result, producers with demonstrable environmental credentials may be able to maintain wider market access (e.g., deforestation-free supply) or premium pricing on their products (Meyer and Miller, 2015; Audubon, 2026). Further, there are opportunities for producers to engage with both government- and private-sector-led voluntary schemes aiming to improve environmental outcomes, including agri-environmental stewardship schemes and carbon and biodiversity markets (Whish et al., 2016). The beef industry will be key to achieving positive outcomes for biodiversity given the substantial land area it occupies (Gilbert et al., 2018), particularly in landscapes where ecosystems and species of conservation concern are concentrated. To provide assurance around the environmental benefits of beef sustainability initiatives, we need robust, high-integrity measurements of the state of biodiversity and ecosystem function. Ideally, such measures would provide a streamlined, consistent approach to measuring biodiversity across different beef-production regions that has relevance both to producers at the local scale and processors, manufacturers, retailers, and brands at broader regional and global scales. In early 2026, the Global Roundtable for Sustainable Beef (GRSB) published a report aiming to highlight metrics that are commonly used in global ecosystem accounting and biodiversity monitoring frameworks (GRSB, 2026). This report was developed with the intention of improving clarity within the beef industry regarding what metrics may be required or desired to demonstrate nature-positive outcomes within beef-producing regions. The report highlighted that measurements of ecosystem extent and ecosystem condition, alongside measures of priority species, would provide information relevant to downstream supply chain actors in alignment with global reporting frameworks while also being relevant to farm and landscape-level projects. However, to leverage the full value of ecosystem extent and ecosystem condition metrics for reporting and decision-making, two key challenges remain. First, access to this information by downstream actors is often restricted by a lack of comprehensive traceability systems in many beef-producing regions. It is often where downstream actors have the poorest visibility in their supply chains (due to indirect supply) that challenges to ecosystem condition or extent (like deforestation) can occur (zu Ermgassen et al., 2022). Without this visibility, it can be difficult for downstream actors to implement actions that help address these challenges, like the incentivization of science-based land management practices. Second, actions to improve ecosystem extent and condition are implemented and often measured at the farm-level but must be scaled to broader resolutions to be most useful for global supply chains and government applications. In response to these challenges, landscape and jurisdictional approaches (LJAs) are increasingly being used in key commodity production regions (SourceUp, 2026). Landscape approaches are multi-stakeholder initiatives that aim to advance shared sustainability goals and build resilience within a defined geographic area (ISEAL, 2026). Jurisdictional initiatives associate the geographic area with political boundaries with the purpose of using strong government representation to ensure public policy is aligned with the goals of the landscape approach. Landscape initiatives can refer to coordinated efforts within either political boundaries or environmental delineations (such as within watersheds). Since many of the drivers of loss of biodiversity and ecosystem functioning often occur on a landscape scale, like habitat loss and fragmentation (Bennett et al., 2006), landscape initiatives have the potential to address these threatening processes on the same scale at which they occur. They also provide important geographic focal points for processors, manufacturers, retailers, and brands to provide a way to prioritize action and investment at a geographic scale where traceability is incomplete (zu Ermgassen et al., 2022). At a global level, there is significant interest from the private sector to increase the number of hectares under LJAs, including in beef-producing landscapes. For instance, the Consumer Goods Forum’s Forest Positive Coalition—made up of retailers and manufacturers from around the world—prioritize beef as one of its core commodities, with one of their overarching ambitions to have “landscapes that implement and monitor sustainable land use policies that enable responsible commodity production, protect forests and natural ecosystems, respect human rights of local communities and workers, and strengthen their livelihoods” (Consumer Goods Forum, 2023, p. 18). However, LJAs that focus on a single dimension of a landscape (e.g., beef production or conservation outcomes) may not achieve this goal as effectively as those that seek to integrate more sectors and stakeholders operating within the landscape and across different scales of governance (Carmenta et al., 2020). With growing interest in the Nature-Positive concept, understanding how nature-related metrics may be applied within LJAs to demonstrate outcomes and foster stakeholder alignment around landscape-level targets and actions is increasingly important. To date, the literature surrounding LJAs has not examined the potential benefits of adopting a landscape-level approach to improving biodiversity and ecosystem functions in beef-producing landscapes or how ecosystem accounting metrics can be applied within LJAs in alignment with Nature-Positive principles.
