Abstract. Long-term monitoring of gross primary production (GPP) is essential for quantifying terrestrial carbon uptake and ecosystem responses to climate variability and extremes. VODCA2GPP is a data-driven upscaling framework that links eddy-covariance (EC) GPP observations to passive-microwave vegetation optical depth (VOD), together with reanalysis air temperature, providing a multi-decadal microwave-based complement to optical GPP products. However, its reliance on reanalysis temperature reduces the methodological independence of the microwave-based estimate, and its sensitivity to water stress is limited in some ecosystems. Here, we develop and evaluate an updated microwave-driven GPP framework in which the time-varying environmental drivers are derived from microwave observations. At the same time, static land-cover information provides biome context. The framework produces 8-day GPP at 0.25° spatial resolution over 2002–2020. Using a sequence of Random Forest (RF) models trained to upscale EC GPP, we test the incremental contribution of different predictor groups. We replace ERA5-Land 2-m air temperature (T2M) with land-surface temperature (LST) derived from harmonised Ka-band brightness temperatures from AMSR-E, AMSR2, and SSMIS F17, and then evaluate land-cover (LC) fractions as biome context, a spatially varying multi-year mean of L-band VOD as persistent canopy-structure information, and surface soil moisture (SSM) and root-zone soil moisture (RZSM) as shallow and deeper water-availability constraints. The models are compared with external GPP products, sun-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF), and drought-related datasets. Predictive skill is assessed using site-grouped 10-fold cross-validation, keeping all observations from a site together in either the training or validation set within each fold. Replacing reanalysis T2M with microwave-derived LST yielded broadly comparable site-level predictive performance. Adding LC fractions produces the largest individual improvement in predictive skill (median r: 0.690 to 0.762; RMSE: 2.646 to 2.345 g C m−2 d−1), while the spatially varying multi-year L-band VOD mean provides a smaller additional improvement by adding persistent canopy-structure information. Structural and hydrological constraints improve agreement with external GPP products, SIF, and drought indicators, with the clearest gains in short-vegetation and water-limited regions; among the hydrological predictors, RZSM provides the strongest improvement. The best-performing configuration achieves a median site-level correlation of r = 0.798 and an RMSE of 2.294 g C m−2 d−1. Despite these improvements, the GPP magnitude of our models remains systematically higher than in the comparison products. Overall, the results show that the updated framework can reproduce long-term GPP dynamics without reanalysis-based temperature forcing, while static LC fractions provide complementary biome context. Among the added predictors, LC fractions provide the largest overall gain in predictive skill and help distinguish productivity among vegetation types, the multi-year L-band VOD mean adds persistent canopy-structure information, and RZSM improves the representation of water-limited GPP variability, especially at short-vegetation sites. Remaining limitations include the mismatch between EC footprints and the much coarser satellite grid, uneven environmental and geographic coverage of the tower network, and environmental controls on GPP that are not explicitly represented by the current predictor set.

The research consists of the analysis of the detection of overshooting tops (OT) over a period of 10 years using water vapour imagery from a satellite. OT is usually observed in thunderstorms producing severe hail. The results were compared with other remote sensing data (weather radar and lightning) to validate the algorithm and to characterise those severe thunderstorms correctly identified. First, it was observed how the algorithm detects false OT associated with non-convective structures, mainly during the non-warm season. Because the differences between the satellite parameters in well- and badly-corrected overshooting tops are small, with an average minimum brightness temperature difference of less than 2 °C, it is difficult to distinguish correct cases from incorrect ones using satellite imagery alone. For this reason, it is highly recommended to combine it with other data types, as in the present analysis. In warm-season cases, the results show that OT signatures were well identified in most cases, but there are cases with elevated false alarm ratios or low probabilities of detection. Finally, the characterisation of severe thunderstorms combining multiple systems led to the quantification of different parameters from different points of view, showing that TOP45 and electrification provide better results. Events with high electrification occur mainly in the warm season, while those without flashes were detected during the cold season. These results are relevant to improving the forecast of severe events in Catalonia.

Abstract. Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) present a significant hazard in warming alpine environments, but detailed, sub-seasonal studies of ice-dammed glacier lakes remain rare due to data scarcity. To overcome this challenge, we reconstruct nearly a decade (2016–2025) of drainage timings, outburst volumes, lake levels, and automated, machine learning-based sub-seasonal lake refilling cycles at the ice-dammed lake Nedre Demmevatnet (southwestern Norway), dammed by the glacier Rembesdalskåka, an outlet glacier of the Hardangerjøkulen ice cap. By integrating publicly available satellite and meteorological datasets, we evaluate remote sensing capabilities and establish an error budget for tracking a small and highly dynamic water body. We validate our spaceborne findings using field measurements, including water-level loggers, time-lapse cameras, a local automatic weather station, and high-resolution UAV photogrammetry, complemented by PlanetScope imagery. Combining Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery, we constrain GLOF drainage windows to ± 2 days. Lake volume sensitivity tests revealed that while satellite outline errors are minor (2.6–4.2 %), using the static regional digital elevation model ArcticDEM (2014) causes a 25.5 % volume underestimation compared to our 2022 UAV bathymetry due to rapid ice-dam retreat and lakebed erosion. Crucially, the time gap between the last cloud-free satellite image and the GLOF introduces a relative daily volume underestimation of 1.7 %, which scales up significantly during cloudy periods. Our validated multi-sensor remote sensing approach enables valuable glaciological insights, revealing that GLOF timings shifted earlier by an average of 10 days, alongside shortened refilling periods over the past 9 years. Between 2016 and 2022, pre-GLOF lake levels reached 1236–1239 m a.s.l., closely matching the theoretical hydrostatic flotation threshold. In contrast, the 2023 event drained at approximately 1224 m a.s.l. – more than 10 m below this threshold – following a shortened melt period indicated by fewer positive degree days, possibly due to opening of subglacial channels through melt. Finally, we synthesize the workflow developed and tested on our case study into an operational framework that facilitates transferability to other rapidly changing ice-dammed lakes.

Accurate crop area mapping underpins agricultural planning, food security and irrigation management, yet government records, satellite imagery, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) surveys and crowdsourced farmer reports each carry distinct limitations in accuracy, scalability, cost and timeliness. This paper reports a systematic review conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020. From 3432 records retrieved through four structured queries, 350 peer-reviewed articles published between 2010 and 2025 were retained after de-duplication, multi-stage relevance scoring and eligibility appraisal. Each study was assigned one primary technology: satellite remote sensing (n = 249, 71.1%), multi-source fusion with satellite data (n = 41, 11.7%), UAV with satellite data (n = 33, 9.4%), standalone UAV (n = 16, 4.6%), UAV with multi-source fusion (n = 7, 2.0%) and crowdsourcing (n = 4, 1.1%). Counted non-exclusively, satellite data appear in 323 of the 350 studies, UAV data in 56 and crowdsourced data in 4. Optical and synthetic aperture radar platforms, UAV sensor suites, participatory platforms and machine-learning classifiers are appraised in turn. The review then sets out the Synergized Mapping framework, which combines administrative records, crowdsourced reports, satellite imagery and UAV surveys in a cost-ordered iterative validation sequence, and illustrates it at Loni Devkar, Maharashtra, India. There, government records understate cultivated area by 57–103% relative to UAV, crowdsourced and satellite estimates, leaving 306,975 m³ of crop water requirement unaccounted. Persistent gaps include the scarcity of crowdsourcing research, the absence of standardised accuracy benchmarks across agro-climatic zones, and limited cost–accuracy optimisation for smallholder systems.

This repository provides the code and datasets corresponding to the manuscript "Advancing satellite remote sensing from open water mapping to water type classification and hydrographic characterization: Application to the endorheic Tibetan Plateau", and includes two folders:Water type product: This folder contains the water type classification for the endorheic Tibetan Plateau during the mean annual discharge period (October) from 2014 to 2021. The water types are coded as follows: 1 = river networks; 2 = isolated lakes; 3 = pathway lakes; 4 = terminal lakes. In addition, this folder includes river width sampling points. The attribute table of the river width points provides river width (width_yyyy), braided index (BI_yyyy), drainage area (Ad_km), and stream order (Sorder) for the mean annual discharge period from 2014 to 2021.Codes: This folder contains Python and MATLAB codes for water type classification and hydrographic characterization of river networks. It includes three subfolders corresponding to the three parts of the workflow described in the manuscript, with the execution order explicitly indicated.

Chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) is a key indicator of phytoplankton biomass and freshwater quality and is strongly influenced by nutrient availability, seasonal variability and climatic conditions. This study investigates the spatiotemporal dynamics of Chl-a in Chitgar Lake, an artificial urban lake in Tehran, Iran, by integrating long-term in-situ observations (2013–2025) with satellite-derived estimates from Sentinel-2 and Landsat-8. Seasonal analysis revealed that Chl-a concentrations were highest during summer (mean: 2.93 mg/m³), peaking in August (3.53 mg/m³), coinciding with elevated water temperatures (up to 30.8°C) and reduced dissolved oxygen (mean: 8.35 mg/L), indicative of eutrophic conditions. In contrast, winter and spring exhibited lower Chl-a levels associated with cooler temperatures and more stable oxygen conditions. The mean total phosphorus concentration (0.03 mg/L) suggests phosphorus limitation, consistent with international eutrophication thresholds. Four satellite-based algorithms – Two-Band Ratio, Normalized Difference Chlorophyll Index (NDCI), Three-Band Difference Algorithm (3BDA), and Maximum Chlorophyll Index (MCI) – were evaluated using S2 and L8 imagery. Sentinel-2 consistently outperformed Landsat-8, with NDCI achieving RMSE of 1.23 mg/m³, MAE of 0.93 mg/m³, and R² of 0.68. Seasonal validation identified fall as the most reliable period for Chl-a estimation (RMSE: 0.88–1.03 mg/m³), while winter showed the lowest errors but limited explanatory power (R²: 0.23–0.28). Landsat-8 yielded acceptable performance, particularly in spring (R²: 0.64–0.84), despite its coarser spatial resolution. Spatial Chl-a maps derived from NDCI revealed consistent distribution patterns between satellites and strong agreement with in-situ measurements. However, Sentinel-2’s finer spatial resolution (10–20 m) enabled improved detection of small-scale variability. Overall, the results highlight the value of Sentinel-2 red-edge bands for Chl-a retrieval in optically complex inland waters, while confirming the continued importance of Landsat-8 for long-term trend analysis. The findings emphasize the need for local calibration and support integrated satellite – in-situ monitoring frameworks for improved eutrophication management in urban lakes.

Abstract. The palsa mires – hummocks with a permafrost core – of northern Finland are among the southernmost periglacial features in the Northern Hemisphere and mark the southern boundary of permafrost range. The rapid warming of circumpolar regions demands a better understand of the complex of environmental changes in the marginal permafrost zone. The study aims to investigate changes in selected environmental features (vegetation, water conditions and land moisture) in northern Finland in the years 1985–2024 using Landsat satellite data, with particular emphasis on the differences taking place in palsa mires. The calculated spectral indices NDVI, NDWI, MNDWI, NDMI and LST were analysed in relation to each other and to environmental data. The analysis of changes in spectral indices over time showed a small but systematic increase in the vegetation index value, an increase in soil moisture, and varied responses in indices related to surface water. Principal component analysis (PCA), linear mixed-effects models (LMM) and redundancy analysis (RDA) indicated the multidimensional structure of remote sensing indices and revealed the main environmental factors determining changes in vegetation and moisture in the study area. One of the main predictors differentiating the spectral response was determined to be palsa mires, which differed from mineral soils, but also from other organic soils. The results confirmed the effectiveness of RS and multispectral indices based on Landsat data for studying environmental changes, while indicating the need for multidimensional analyses that include various indicators and local environmental predictors.

Land use and land cover (LULC) changes in the Amazon are among the main drivers of biodiversity loss, ecosystem degradation, and the intensification of climate change. This study aimed to analyze the multitemporal dynamics of LULC around the Jamanxim River, Pará, Brazilian Amazon, between 2015 and 2025, using high-resolution imagery from the CBERS-4/PAN satellite. The study area covers 492.74 km², including part of the Jamanxim National Forest, a conservation unit under strong pressure from agricultural expansion and logging activities. The methodology included geometric correction of the images, Gram–Schmidt pansharpening, and supervised classification with the Random Forest algorithm, validated with historical imagery from Google Earth Pro. Thematic maps of land use and cover were generated, and performance metrics such as overall accuracy, omission and commission errors, and F1-scores were assessed. The results indicated a significant reduction in forest cover, from 412.28 km² in 2015 to 355.47 km² in 2025 (–13.78%). Non-vegetated areas increased by 132.47%, while agricultural areas expanded by 54.97%. The forest and water body classes showed high accuracy (F1-score > 0.95), while confusion persisted between agricultural and bare soil classes. Overall accuracy remained above 90% across all years, with the highest performance recorded in 2020 (96.31%). These results highlight the potential of CBERS-4/PAN imagery for monitoring multitemporal changes in tropical forest landscapes. At the same time, they reveal the intensification of deforestation and the growing threats to conservation in the Amazon, reinforcing the importance of remote sensing for environmental management and policy support.

Pakistan's agricultural sector faces a growing water crisis, exacerbated by climate variability, over-extraction of groundwater, and misalignment between traditional irrigation scheduling and actual crop needs. Because 90% of the country's freshwater is used for irrigation, developing tools to improve water-use efficiency is essential to achieving food and water security. Early forecasting of crop-specific irrigation demand allows farmers, irrigation managers, and policymakers to align water supply with dynamic field requirements, optimize canal operations, and reduce water wastage. Early forecasting of crop irrigation demand enhances water efficiency and supports food security. Accurate irrigation forecasts enable farmers and decision-makers to schedule irrigation based on crop types and climate conditions, ensuring crops receive adequate water. Traditional biophysical models predict growth based on climate, soil, and irrigation factors, often assuming fixed water delivery schedules. These models focus on broad hydrological trends but lack tailored irrigation forecasts for specific crop stages. While machine learning (ML) has been applied to predict yield and biomass, forecasts of crop water requirements have been overlooked. The availability of cloud platforms such as Google Earth Engine (GEE) has revolutionized large-scale geospatial analysis, enabling timely, spatially resolved forecasting of agricultural irrigation demand. This is crucial for sustainable water use and agricultural resilience. GEE's cloud computing capabilities allow for parallel processing, reducing the need for local storage or high-performance computing infrastructure. Additionally, integrating remote sensing (RS) data archives with ML models and scalable application services creates a powerful environment for operational, data-driven irrigation applications. While many RS-based studies in GEE have focused on land use and crop classification, few have developed operational tools for irrigation forecasting using integrated climate and satellite information. This study addresses that gap by developing a cloud-based irrigation forecasting system within GEE, integrated with Google for training and testing geospatial remote sensing datasets to generate early irrigation forecasts. The system integrates multi-sensor satellite data, including Landsat-8, Sentinel-2, and PlanetScope, with archival datasets from 2015 to 2025 at 30 m, 10 m, and 3 m spatial resolutions, respectively, and combines them with climate information. A Random Forest (RF) machine learning model was implemented and trained using an 80-20% split to estimate crop-specific water requirements, measured as actual evapotranspiration (ETact), across spatial and temporal scales. The framework automates data retrieval and irrigation forecast generation, demonstrating GEE's potential as a cloud-native platform for real-time agricultural water management. Trained models demonstrated high validation accuracy for NDVI (R² = 0.9224), LST (R² = 0.8602), Rn (R² = 0.84), and SAVI (R² = 0.87). Models such as Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), XGBoost, and Random Forest were trained using an 80-20 train-test split. CNN achieved the highest R² of 0.89, followed by XGBoost (R² = 0.81) and Random Forest (R² = 0.76). These predicted variables served as inputs to an RF model that estimated ETact, the core metric used to calculate irrigation demand. The irrigation forecast was tested over two cropping seasons (Kharif and Rabi) using observed ET data from an Eddy Covariance Flux Tower. For rice in Kharif, CNN predicted 6.798 mm/day (flux tower: 6.99 mm/day), and for wheat in Rabi, CNN predicted 2.041 mm/day (observed: 1.86 mm/day). In wheat’s growth phase, CNN forecasted 29.87 mm/day, close to the flux tower’s 33 mm/day. Overall, CNN outperformed other models across various crops, showing strong spatial and temporal accuracy. The forecasting information was applied to wheat cropping systems during the Rabi season. Weekly ET maps generated by the system supported precise and timely irrigation scheduling. Integrating satellite-derived biophysical variables into the GEE cloud-based application system enables informed decision-making for farmers, extension agents, and water managers to advance sustainable water resource planning amid increasing climate variability.

Abstract. Characterizing the moist thermodynamic structure of the lower troposphere (LT) from spaceborne observations is challenging. This is largely due to the LT's highly variable moisture distribution which requires high-resolution observations in both the vertical and horizontal dimensions. Two of the most impactful spaceborne remote sensing technologies in numerical weather prediction (NWP) are (1) the global navigation satellite system – radio occultation (GNSS-RO) and (2) nadir sounding instruments which include microwave radiometers (MWR) and infrared sounders (IR). These two technologies provide complementary information of atmospheric temperature and water vapor. GNSS-RO provides high vertical resolution (∼200 m) with near zero interference from hydrometeor, but its horizontal resolution along the ray path is coarse (>100 km). On the other hand, nadir sounders measure brightness temperature (TB) that can be related to the temperature and water vapor structure in the atmospheric column with higher horizontal resolution (∼25 km). However, retrievals from passive sounders have lower vertical resolution (>2 km), and are complicated by precipitation, clouds, and surface emissivity uncertainty over land. In this study we combine these two complementary types of observations by use of a novel tomography method to improve the 3D characterization of water vapor in the LT. This is done by adjusting the water vapor density along the RO links to match the RO observations, while preserving the horizontal water vapor variability based on information derived from the nadir sounders. We test this method using simulations based on mesoscale model outputs from the Weather Research and Forecasting Model (WRF), as well as real observations from RO and Cross-track Infrared Microwave Sounder Suite (CrIMSS). We demonstrate that the tomographic retrieval can resolve the complex moisture structure better than what is possible from either measurement alone.

This report presents a multi-sensor satellite remote sensing analysis of the Irtyash-Kyshtym-Kasli corridor, Chelyabinsk Oblast, Russia (center: 55.458376°N, 60.596717°E). The study was conducted from Mombasa, Kenya on 22 October 2026. Data used:- Sentinel-1C IW GRD Scene 1471 (22 October 2026) - VV/VH backscatter analysis- ICESat-2 ATL08 Land and Vegetation Height- GEDI L2A Canopy Height and Ground Elevation- Optical basemap for contextual reference Study Area: Lake Irtyash, Kyshtym, Kasli, Ozyorsk, Metlino, Mayak Production Association, and Special Water Reservoir B-11. Dense forest with extensive hydrological network. Key Findings:Analysis of Sentinel-1C backscatter reveals linear moisture corridors and hydrologic lineaments that preserve evidence of former landscape organization. This includes relic field divisions, former industrial perimeters, and drainage alignments. Linear moisture boundaries often follow anthropogenic linear features: old enclosure walls, drainage ditches, causeways and territorial boundaries. The radar visibility of such wet corridors, invisible in summer optical imagery, provides a basis for tracing wall continuities across forested ground. Forestry Reference: Quadrants Ar_kv_114 and Ar_kv_115, Kyshtym Forest District. Figures included:Figure 1 - ICESat-2 ATL08 tracks over study areaFigure 2 - GEDI canopy height measurementsFigure 3 - Sentinel-1C Scene 1471 selectionFigure 4 - Sentinel-1C 1471 VV/VH backscatter moisture analysis

The use of remote sensing in crop and soil management is instrumental. Satellite images of agricultural fields were obtained from the Planet explorer account. Vegetation and soil indices, i.e. normalized difference vegetation index, normalized difference water index, soil adjusted vegetation index, have been calculated for crop and soil health monitoring. The analysis focused on identifying key vegetation and soil parameters that influence crop health and productivity. Vegetation indices imagery can assist in monitoring crops, such as rice, potato, and wheat crops. To establish a relationship between vegetation indices and soil parameters, a quadratic regression model is applied. The model interpolated vegetation indices with soil properties including nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, moisture, pH, and electrical conductivity. Curve-fitting techniques using quadratic regression model strengthen the interrelations between the indices and the soil parameters. The model performance was computed using mean squared error (MSE) and R-squared (R²) values. The R² varied for each soil parameter, showing that the model accuracy varied for each. Differences between model predictions and actual measurements indicate that more refinements need to be made. A possible enhancement is the incorporation of nanosensors for real-time, in-situ measurement of some of the most important soil parameters such as nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, moisture content, pH, and electrical conductivity. These nanosensors can yield highly localized and sensitive data, which can act as reliable ‘ground truth’ to cross-validate and complement satellite-based observations.

This repository contains Python and Google Earth Engine scripts supporting the analysis of global hydropower reservoir expansion and associated soil moisture variability during 2003–2020. The study examines surface-water dynamics across 231 hydropower reservoir sites worldwide, with detailed multi-source remote-sensing assessments conducted for 20 selected reservoirs. The code covers six main analytical components: (1) global reservoir surface-water expansion screening using JRC Global Surface Water data; (2) Landsat-based water extraction using NDWI, MNDWI, and AWEIsh; (3) spatial sensitivity analysis of reservoir water-area estimates; (4) ERA5-Land soil moisture variability and trend analysis; (5) matched-grid comparisons and climate-adjusted statistical modeling; and (6) robustness and sensitivity assessments of soil moisture responses. The repository includes analysis scripts, documentation of data requirements, software dependencies, and recommended execution procedures. The scripts are provided to facilitate reproducibility and further methodological evaluation. They represent a preliminary reconstruction of the analytical procedures and require configuration, input data, and validation against the final manuscript results before they can be considered fully reproducible. Original satellite imagery, reanalysis datasets, and reservoir metadata are not included and should be obtained from their respective data providers.

Abstract. Thermal infrared (TIR) satellite remote sensing is essential for monitoring land surface temperature (LST) and surface energy fluxes, supporting applications in hydrology, agriculture, climate, and urban climate. Existing TIR missions—such as LANDSAT, ASTER, ECOSTRESS, and Sentinel-3 SLSTR—offer complementary capabilities but remain constrained by trade-offs between spatial resolution, revisit frequency, and radiometric accuracy, limiting their ability to capture rapidly evolving surface processes at field to regional scales. The TRISHNA (Thermal Infrared Satellite for High-Resolution Natural Resource Assessment) mission, expected in 2027, addresses this gap by providing 60 m TIR imagery over a ~1000 km swath with sub-weekly revisit, enabling systematic monitoring of surface energy processes in natural and managed ecosystems. Its integrated design —including orbit configuration, spectral channels (VNIR, SWIR, TIR), viewing geometry, and calibration strategy— supports accurate retrievals of evapotranspiration, vegetation water stress, and surface temperature dynamics. Synergies with upcoming missions such as ESA’s Land Surface Temperature Mission (LSTM) and NASA’s EAGLE mission (Explorer for Artemis Geology Lunar and Earth) will enhance temporal coverage, cross-calibration, and long-term data continuity.

This thesis references bathymetry data and chemical composition, grain size distribution, and suspended load data of sediment from the Gulf of Alaska. The aforementioned data are referenced in citation: Burbank, D. C. 1974. Suspended Sediment Transport and Deposition in Alaskan Coastal Waters: With Special Emphasis on Remote Sensing by ERTS-1 Satellite. M.S. Thesis, Institute of Marine Science, University of Alaska, Fairbanks, Alaska. 222 pp. This literature was collected as part of a metadatabase that represents one or more nearshore resources (from physical attributes such as water and air, to birds and mammals). Each entry is viewable in three formats, 1) a geospatial explicit format (ArcView 3.3) named GIS ArcView 3.3 Near GEM project, 2) a spreadsheet format (Excel 2002 and within ArcView) named GEM Nearshore Metadata Set, and 3) a ProCite database named GEM Nearshore Metadata References, which consists of references included in 1 and 2 above. The ProCite database record number corresponds to the Excel Procite Number. Reference Procite #150 for this literature's metadata. The metadata are maintained in digital format (ArcView 3.3, Excel 2002, and Procite) and are available from the Alaska Science Center, USGS in Anchorage, Alaska. For a detailed description of the three databases and the project, see "Bodkin, J. L., and T. Dean. 2003. Alternative Sampling Designs for Nearshore Monitoring (Gulf Ecosystem Monitoring and Research Project G-030687), US Geological Survey, Alaska Science Center, Anchorage, Alaska." available on-line at http://www.evostc.state.ak.us/pdf/GEM_final_reports/030687.pdf. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

Growing competition for water has intensified the push for efficient irrigation management. As crop growth and soil properties vary at sub-field scales, irrigation management zones are developed and monitored using in situ data and vegetation indices (VIs). The latter has limited ability to capture plant water stress due to bare soil interference, crop-specific spectral differences, and a time lag between stress onset and phenological response to water stress. Remote sensing evapotranspiration (ET) data can supplement VIs to better characterize water stress. Here, we develop the Water Stress Index (WSI), a satellite-based index that identifies areas of water stress relative to the rest of the field over a selected period using an energy balance approach. The WSI is derived from ET and solar radiation data. An energy use proxy (latent heat flux from OpenET ensemble model) is subtracted from an energy availability proxy (LiDAR-derived and gridMET-modeled incoming solar radiation), producing a gridded map of relative water stress. The downscaled energy availability proxy provides field-scale variability that can be compared with high-resolution ET estimates more effectively than traditional, coarse-resolution products. The WSI is evaluated against in situ matric potential data and multi-season yield data. Results show the WSI consistently outperforms VIs and OpenET in describing end-of-season winter wheat yield. VIs outperform the WSI and OpenET for potatoes, which could be related to potatoes complex and rapid growth patterns. By leveraging energy balance concepts and accessible remote sensing products, the WSI offers an adaptable framework for identifying water-stressed areas in irrigated agricultural fields.

Abstract Accurate forecasting of shoreline evolution is important for coastal monitoring and management, particularly in dynamic and data-scarce environments. This study investigates a modular framework, applied to Icapuí, northeastern Brazil, that integrates multi-temporal Landsat imagery, remote-sensing-based shoreline extraction, linear regression, and a hybrid convolutional neural network–long short-term memory (CNN–LSTM) architecture. Two distinct Landsat temporal datasets were used for the statistical and deep-learning experiments, and no regression-generated imagery was incorporated into CNN–LSTM training or evaluation. Water–land boundaries were derived from observed Landsat imagery using the Modified Normalized Difference Water Index (MNDWI) followed by binary classification. For spatio-temporal modelling, the CNN–LSTM operated directly on sequences of observed MNDWI rasters to predict the raster corresponding to the subsequent time step. Model performance was evaluated using MAE and RMSE in normalized MNDWI raster-value units, which quantify raster reconstruction error rather than shoreline-position error in physical units. Predicted MNDWI rasters were subsequently converted into binary water–land representations from which vector shorelines were derived for spatial interpretation. Across the analysed coastal sectors, some three-timestep configurations produced lower reconstruction errors than their two-timestep counterparts, suggesting that additional temporal context may provide useful information for raster reconstruction within the analysed sequence. The out-of-series 2023 forecast showed spatially variable behaviour among coastal sectors and was treated as an exploratory model-derived scenario because no corresponding observed target was available for independent validation. Overall, the study provides a proof-of-concept assessment of integrating satellite-derived coastal observations with spatio-temporal deep learning under sparse temporal data availability, while highlighting the need for denser observations, independent temporal validation, and metric-domain shoreline evaluation before robust long-term forecasting capability can be established.

As an important ecologically sensitive zone and ecological security barrier in northern China, the agro-pastoral ecotone of Inner Mongolia has an ecological pattern and security status that are closely related to regional sustainable development. Based on satellite remote sensing, land-cover, and meteorological observation data from 2000 to 2023, this study applied an ecological pattern transition matrix, vegetation models, and the PSR framework to quantitatively analyze regional ecosystem transitions, ecological function evolution, and ecological security risks. The results showed that from 1990 to 2023, forest and grassland areas increased, desert, water body, and wetland areas decreased, and settlements exhibited a sharp expansion trend. From 2000 to 2023, the region exhibited an apparent warming tendency and a statistically significant wetting trend. NPP and NDVI displayed an increasing spatial distribution from northwest to southeast. For the independently observed NDVI, correlation with precipitation (r = 0.823) was markedly higher than with temperature (r = 0.141). Correlation coefficients for model-simulated NPP against climate variables should be interpreted with caution because precipitation and temperature are explicit inputs within the NPP empirical-statistical model. The ecological security index of the study area generally increased, while the response subsystem continued to decline after 2005. The security levels showed spatial differentiation characterized by security in the northeast, insecurity in the southwest, and critical status in the central region, and the areas showing improvement gradually expanded from 2000 to 2023. In addition, feasible and constructive ecological restoration and regulation strategies were proposed for different regions. This study reveals the evolutionary characteristics and potential influencing mechanisms of regional ecological patterns and security, providing support for the construction of the ecological security barrier in northern China.

Abstract Bellandur Lake in Bangalore, India represents one of the most severely polluted urban water bodies in South Asia, necessitating systematic monitoring for environmental management. This study employed Sentinel-2 Multispectral Instrument imagery to assess spatiotemporal variations in water quality parameters from January 2023 to December 2025. Six water quality indicators were derived using established remote sensing algorithms: chlorophyll-a (estimated using the Normalised Difference Chlorophyll Index as the primary method), turbidity, total suspended solids, coloured dissolved organic matter, Secchi depth, and floating algae index. A total of 100 Sentinel-2 images were processed using Google Earth Engine, yielding 93 valid observations across 28 months after excluding monsoon periods affected by cloud cover and confining analysis to complete years 2023–2025. Results indicated severely degraded conditions with mean NDCI-based chlorophyll-a of 71.31 µg/L (median 70.24 µg/L), consistently classifying the lake as hypereutrophic. Mann–Kendall trend analysis revealed statistically significant increasing trends in chlorophyll-a ( τ = 0.144, p = 0.041) and floating algae index ( τ = 0.419, p < 0.001), with concurrent significant decreasing trends in turbidity ( p < 0.001) and total suspended solids ( p = 0.001). Pixel-wise FDR-corrected trend analysis identified 33.7% of the lake area exhibiting significant increasing chlorophyll-a trends. The lake consistently exceeded Central Pollution Control Board standards, with 100% of observations surpassing permissible total suspended solids limits and 98.9% of observations classified as hypereutrophic. These findings are interpreted as indicative of relative spatial and temporal patterns given the absence of site-specific in situ calibration; however, they provide valuable baseline information for management interventions and demonstrate the utility of satellite remote sensing for monitoring polluted urban water bodies.

The growing demand for food, pressure on natural resources, and increasing climate variability have strengthened interest in data-driven agriculture. Artificial intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, satellite imagery, and decision-support platforms can help farmers monitor crop conditions and allocate water, fertilizer, and labour more precisely. This paper proposes an integrated AI-based smart agriculture framework that combines field sensing, remote observation, weather information, farm records, and machine-learning analytics. The framework is intended to support soil-moisture assessment, irrigation scheduling, crop-stress detection, pest and disease screening, yield estimation, and farm-level resource planning. Its workflow includes data acquisition, quality checks, feature engineering, model development, recommendations, and feedback from field observations. The paper also considers practical constraints, including limited connectivity, sensor calibration, small and fragmented datasets, model generalization, affordability, privacy, and farmer trust. Because no field dataset or controlled trial was supplied for this study, the paper presents a conceptual architecture and an evaluation plan rather than measured performance claims. A future pilot should compare the proposed system with local baseline practices using metrics such as water use per unit area, crop yield, input costs, alert precision and recall, and farmer usability. AI can contribute to more informed agricultural decisions when recommendations are locally validated, understandable, and designed around the needs of farmer.

Abstract. Chlorophyll is a crucial climate variable and remotely sensed satellite chlorophyll estimates are essential to understanding large-scale biological processes. Current ocean color chlorophyll algorithms, however, are less accurate in optically complex inland and coastal waters. As a result, remote sensing algorithms are not able to fully resolve chlorophyll concentrations in optically complex coastal regions leading to greater uncertainty in regions of high productivity. This can further lead to errors in regional biogeochemical models and hinder fisheries and ecosystem monitoring and research. In order to develop more accurate coastal chlorophyll retrievals, in situ chlorophyll measurements are needed for algorithm calibration and validation. Here the methods used to develop a single cohesive standardized in situ chlorophyll, chromophoric dissolved organic matter (CDOM), and remote sensing reflectance (Rrs) dataset from multiple public data repositories are described. The final product is a North American dataset of quality controlled chlorophyll measurements and associated metadata. The dataset includes more than 700,000 chlorophyll values with coincidental CDOM and Rrs data when available. Methodological flags such as chlorophyll measurement method, triplicate samples, and in vitro/in vivo flags distinguish between data collection methods. The dataset includes regularly formatted metadata across all sources to ensure due credit to the programs collecting the samples. The resulting dataset is then matched to satellite chlorophyll data to examine the difference in chlorophyll retrievals across multiple water types and regions. This dataset is currently being used to validate a new coastal chlorophyll algorithm in development and to assess chlorophyll retrievals. All methods and data are publicly available at doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20140178 (Milton et al., 2026).
