Surface water change is a very important indicator for environmental, climatic, and anthropogenic activities. The sediment brought by the stream into the reservoir starts settling down and gets deposited on the bed of the reservoir at all levels. The finer particles are carried in suspension and settle down on the reservoir floor while some of these are passed over the spillway towards the downstream of a dam. If the concentration is high, density current occurs along the floor of the reservoir. The purpose of this study is to assess the sedimentation of the Poondi Reservoir using Satellite Remote-Sensing (SRS). This helps in providing full utilization capacity of reservoir by providing more storage and supply of fresh water to the catchment area. The sedimentation assessment was carried out using satellite data and reservoir water level data from 2000 to 2020. Water spread area was analyzed from satellite data. The NDWI has been used to delineate open water features and to enhance the presence of water surface and linear interpolation/extrapolation technique has been applied for water spread area at different elevation. Further, these areas were used to compute live storage capacity of reservoir between two elevations by Prismoidal formula.

Large-scale flooding causes widespread disaster, and harmful pollutant concentration in water following flood affects public safety and the environment. In this study, a numerical model for solving the 2D shallow water equations and the solute transport equation is proposed to simulate overland flood and pollutant transport caused by floods. The present model is verified by comparing the predictions with the analytical solutions and simulation results; sufficiently high computational accuracy is achieved. The model is also used to simulate flood inundation and pollution spread in the area of Hun and Taizi Lane (HTL) in China due to river dike breaches; the results show that the coupling model has excellent performance for simulating the flooding process and the temporal and spatial distribution of pollutants in urban or rural areas. We use remote sensing techniques to acquire the land coverage in the area of HTL based on Landsat TM satellites. The impacts of changed land use on mitigation of flooding waves and pollutant spread are investigated; the results indicate that the land cover changes have an obvious influence on the evolution process of flood waves and pollutant transport in the study areas, where the transport of pollutants is very dynamic during flood inundation in HTL area. Furthermore, the motion of pollutants considering anisotropic diffusion is more reasonable than that due to isotropic dispersion in simulating pollutant transport associated with the flood in urban or farmland environments.

Chlorophyll-a concentrations in water bodies are one of the most important environmental evaluation indicators in monitoring the water environment. Small water bodies include headwater streams, springs, ditches, flushes, small lakes, and ponds, which represent important freshwater resources. However, the relatively narrow and fragmented nature of small water bodies makes it difficult to monitor chlorophyll-a via medium-resolution remote sensing. In the present study, we first fused Gaofen-6 (a new Chinese satellite) images to obtain 2 m resolution images with 8 bands, which was approved as a good data source for Chlorophyll-a monitoring in small water bodies as Sentinel-2. Further, we compared five semi-empirical and four machine learning models to estimate chlorophyll-a concentrations via simulated reflectance using fused Gaofen-6 and Sentinel-2 spectral response function. The results showed that the extreme gradient boosting tree model (one of the machine learning models) is the most accurate. The mean relative error (MRE) was 9.03%, and the root-mean-square error (RMSE) was 4.5 mg/m3 for the Sentinel-2 sensor, while for the fused Gaofen-6 image, MRE was 6.73%, and RMSE was 3.26 mg/m3. Thus, both fused Gaofen-6 and Sentinel-2 could estimate the chlorophyll-a concentrations in small water bodies. Since the fused Gaofen-6 exhibited a higher spatial resolution and Sentinel-2 exhibited a higher temporal resolution.

Abstract. The eddy-covariance technique measures carbon, water, and energy fluxes between the land surface and the atmosphere at hundreds of sites globally. Collections of standardised and homogenised flux estimates such as the LaThuile, Fluxnet2015, National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON), Integrated Carbon Observation System (ICOS), AsiaFlux, AmeriFlux, and Terrestrial Ecosystem Research Network (TERN)/OzFlux data sets are invaluable to study land surface processes and vegetation functioning at the ecosystem scale. Space-borne measurements give complementary information on the state of the land surface in the surroundings of the towers. They aid the interpretation of the fluxes and support the benchmarking of terrestrial biosphere models. However, insufficient quality and frequent and/or long gaps are recurrent problems in applying the remotely sensed data and may considerably affect the scientific conclusions. Here, we describe a standardised procedure to extract, quality filter, and gap-fill Earth observation data from the MODIS instruments and the Landsat satellites. The methods consistently process surface reflectance in individual spectral bands, derived vegetation indices, and land surface temperature. A geometrical correction estimates the magnitude of land surface temperature as if seen from nadir or 40∘ off-nadir. Finally, we offer the community living data sets of pre-processed Earth observation data, where version 1.0 features the MCD43A4/A2 and MxD11A1 MODIS products and Landsat Collection 1 Tier 1 and Tier 2 products in a radius of 2 km around 338 flux sites. The data sets we provide can widely facilitate the integration of activities in the eddy-covariance, remote sensing, and modelling fields.

Abstract Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) plans a Phobos sample return mission (MMX: Martian Moons eXploration). In this study, we review the related works on the past climate of Mars, its evolution, and the present climate and weather to describe the scientific goals and strategies of the MMX mission regarding the evolution of the Martian surface environment. The MMX spacecraft will retrieve and return a sample of Phobos regolith back to Earth in 2029. Mars ejecta are expected to be accumulated on the surface of Phobos without being much shocked. Samples from Phobos probably contain all types of Martian rock from sedimentary to igneous covering all geological eras if ejecta from Mars could be accumulated on the Phobos surface. Therefore, the history of the surface environment of Mars can be restored by analyzing the returned samples. Remote sensing of the Martian atmosphere and monitoring ions escaping to space while the spacecraft is orbiting Mars in the equatorial orbit are also planned. The camera with multi-wavelength filters and the infrared spectrometer onboard the spacecraft can monitor rapid transport processes of water vapor, dust, ice clouds, and other species, which could not be traced by the previous satellites on the sun-synchronous polar orbit. Such time-resolved pictures of the atmospheric phenomena should be an important clue to understand both the processes of water exchange between the surface/underground reservoirs and the atmosphere and the drivers of efficient material transport to the upper atmosphere. The mass spectrometer with unprecedented mass resolution can observe ions escaping to space and monitor the atmospheric escape which has made the past Mars to evolve towards the cold and dry surface environment we know today. Together with the above two instruments, it can potentially reveal what kinds of atmospheric events can transport tracers (e.g., H 2 O) upward and enhance the atmospheric escape. Graphical Abstract

Landuse/landcover (LULC) variations play a significant role in the investigation and monitoring of worldwide alterations. LULC and regular adjustments have generally brought about biodiversity misfortune, deforestation, an unnatural weather change, and increased flood events. With the creation of GIS (Geographical Information System) and remote sensing approaches, LULC planning has specified a valuable and comprehensive approach to enhance the choice of zones intended for industrial, urban, and agricultural regions of an area. Various strategies have been designed for extracting information about the earth’s surface by means of image classification, which are commonly divided as supervised and unsupervised classification, based on the availability of reference data. In this chapter, the supervised method of classification has been used to find the available classes. The land use/land cover classification has been done for satellite images of 2000, 2009, 2014, and 2019 through ERDAS IMAGINE 2015 software. It has been identified that land use has undergone major changes from the year 2000 – 2019. The drastic increase of the builtup area or urban area was from 3.12% to 20.25%, an increase in vegetation area was from 8.81% to 19.60%, an increase in water bodies was from 0.24% to 1.12%, while a reduced land cover in agriculture was from 77.24% to 57.44% and a decrease in barren land was from 10.59% to 1.59% from the year 2000 to 2019. This investigation clearly reveals the critical influence of population and its advancement exercises on LULC change. The current examination outlines that GIS and remote sensing are significant advancements for temporal examination and measurement of spatial occurrence, which is generally impractical to endeavor through ordinary planning strategies. Additionally, in this chapter, an attempt has been made to predict the amount of power generation through solar energy by installing solar panels in the identified barren land, which is obtained by image processing technique. It is predicted that 3 MW of power equivalent to around 4800 MWh of solar energy can be generated.

Flood events cause substantial damage to infrastructure and disrupt livelihoods. Timely monitoring of flood extent helps authorities identify severe impacts and plan relief operations. Remote sensing through satellite imagery is an effective method to identify flooded areas. However, critical contextual information about the severity of structural damage or urgent needs of affected population cannot be obtained from remote sensing alone. On the other hand, social sensing through microblogging sites can potentially provide useful information directly from eyewitnesses and affected people. Therefore, this paper explores the integration of remote sensing and social sensing data to derive informed flood extent maps. For this purpose, we employ state-of-the-art deep learning methods to process heterogeneous data obtained from four case-study areas, including two urban regions from Somalia and India and two coastal regions from Italy and The Bahamas. On the remote sensing side, we observe that deep learning models perform generally better than Otsu in flood water prediction. For example, for highly urban areas from Somalia and India, U-Net achieves better F1-scores (0.471 and 0.310, respectively) than Otsu (0.297 and 0.251, respectively). Similarly, for coastal areas, FCN yields a better F1-score for Italy (0.128) than Otsu (0.083) while FCN and Otsu perform on par for The Bahamas (0.102 and 0.105, respectively). Then, on the social sensing side, we add two data layers representing relevant tweet text and images posted from the case-study regions to highlight different ways these heterogeneous data sources complement each other. Our extensive analyses reveal several valuable insights. In particular, we identify three types of signals: (i) confirmatory signals from both sources, which puts greater confidence that a specific region is flooded, (ii) complementary signals that provide different contextual information including needs and requests, disaster impact or damage reports and situational information, and (iii) novel signals when both data sources do not overlap and provide unique information.

Changes in a large-scale glacial lake area directly reflect the regional glacier status and climate changes. However, long time series of glacial lake dataset and comprehensive investigation of the spatiotemporal changes in the glacial lake area in the whole High Mountain Asia (HMA) region remained elusive. Satellite remote sensing provides an indispensable way for dynamic monitoring of glacial lakes over large regions. But glacial lakes are quite small and discretely distributed, and the extraction of glacial lakes is usually influenced by clouds, snow/ice cover, and terrain shadows; thus, there is a lack of an automatic method to continuously monitor the dynamic changes of glacial lakes in a large scale. In this paper, we developed a per-pixel composited method named the “multitemporal mean NDWI composite” to automatically extract the glacial lake area in HMA from 1990 to 2020 using time-series Landsat data. There were 19,294 glacial lakes covering a total area of 1471.85 ± 366.42 k m 2 in 1990, and 22,646 glacial lakes with an area of 1729.08 ± 461.31 k m 2 in 2020. It is noted that the glacial lake area in the whole HMA region expanded by 0.58 ± 0.21 % / a over the past three decades, with high spatiotemporal heterogeneity. The glacial lake area increased at a consistent speed over time. The fastest expansion was in East Kun Lun at an average rate of 2.01 ± 0.54 % / a , while in the Pamir and Hengduan Shan, they show slow increases with rates of 0.33 ± 0.08 % / a and 0.39 ± 0.01 % / a , respectively, during 1990–2020. The greatest increase in lake area occurred at 5000-5200 m a.s.l., which increased by about 45 km 2 (~25%). We conclude that the temperature rise and glacier thinning are the leading factors of glacial lake expansion in HMA, and precipitation is the main source of lake water increase in West Kun Lun. Using the proposed method, a large amount of Landsat images from successive years of melting seasons can be fully utilized to obtain a pixel-level composited cloud-free and solid snow/ice-free glacial lake map. The uncertainties from supraglacial ponds and glacial meltwater were also estimated to improve the reliability and comparability of glacial lake area changes among different regions. This study provides important technical and data support for regional climate changes, glacier hydrology, and disaster analysis.

Automatic extraction of water bodies from various satellite images containing complex targets is a very important and challenging task in remote sensing and image interpretation. In recent years, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become an important choice in the field of semantic segmentation of remote sensing images. However, generic CNN models present many problems when performing water body segmentation, such as: (1) blurred water body boundaries; (2) difficulty in accommodating different scales of rivers, often losing information about many small-scale rivers; and (3) a large number of trainable parameters. This paper proposes an end-to-end CNN structure based on multi-scale residuals and SE-attention for water segmentation, called MRSE-Net. MRSE-Net consists of an encoder-decoder and a skip connection, which captures contextual information at different scales using the encoder, and then passes the encoder feature mapping through the improved skip connection, while localization is achieved by the decoder is implemented. With the multi-scale residual module, the number of parameters in our model can be significantly reduced and water pixels can be extracted accurately. The SE-attention module is used to enhance the prediction results, mitigate the blurring effect, and make the segmented water boundaries more continuous. Landsat-8 images are used to train our model and validate our proposed method’s performance and effectiveness. In addition, we evaluate our method on Landsat-7 and Sentinel-2 images and obtain the best water segmentation results. Preliminary results on Sentinel-2 images show that the cross-sensor generalization capability of our model is beyond the range of the Landsat sensor family.

NASA's Cyclone Global Navigation Satellite System (CYGNSS) mission has gained significant attention within the land remote sensing community for estimating soil moisture (SM) by using the Global Navigation System Reflectometry (GNSS-R) technique. CYGNSS constellation generates Delay-Doppler Maps (DDM)s, containing important earth surface information from GNSS reflection measurements. Many previous studies considered only designed features from CYGNSS DDM such as the peak value of DDM, whereas the whole DDM image is affected by SM, topography, inundation, and overlying vegetation. In this paper, a deep learning (DL)-based framework is presented for estimating SM products in the Continental United States (CONUS) by leveraging spaceborne GNSS-R DDM observations provided by the CYGNSS constellation along with other remotely sensed geophysical data products. A data-driven approach utilizing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) is developed to determine complex relationships between the reflected measurements and surface parameters which can help to provide improved SM estimation. The CNN model is trained jointly with three types of processed DDM images of Analog Power, Effective scattering area, and Bistatic Radar Cross-section (BRCS) with other auxiliary geophysical information such as elevation, soil properties, normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and vegetation water content (VWC). The model is trained and evaluated using from the Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) mission's enhanced SM products at a 9 km × 9 km resolution with VWC less than 5 kg/m$^{2}$. The mean unbiased root-mean-square difference (ubRMSD) between concurrent CYGNSS and SMAP SM retrievals from 2017 to 2020 is 0.0366$m^{3}/m^{3}$with a correlation coefficient of 0.93 over 5-fold cross-validation and 0.0333$m^{3}/m^{3}$with a correlation coefficient of 0.94 over year-based cross-validation at spatial resolution of 9 km × 9 km and temporal resolution same as the CYGNSS mission.

Moderate-high resolution satellite missions provide an opportunity to capture subtle spatial variability in lakes; however, the sparsity of time series for individual satellite instruments cannot monitor temporal variation in the lake environment. To date, studies on the joint observations of chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) in inland lakes from multiple missions have been poorly reported. Here, we generated a harmonized Chl-a dataset for the lakes in the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau in China from 2013 to 2022 by the Landsat 8/9 and Sentinel-2A/B virtual constellation. This study first examined the performance of four atmospheric correction processors to derive remote sensing reflectance (Rrs) from Landsat 8/9 Operational Land Imager (OLI) and Sentinel-2A/B multispectral instrument (MSI) images. We determined that the dark spectral fitting algorithm generated better Rrsthan the other processors, e.g., Rrs(561) mean absolute percentage error (MAPE)=15.2%, Rrs(665) MAPE=27.5%, and Rrs(704) MAPE=25.7%. OLI-derived Rrsat five visible and near-infrared bands showed satisfactory agreement with MSI (slope=0.94, MAPE=11.8%). The mixed density network outperformed the six state-of-the-art algorithms and other two machine learning models in retrieving Chl-a [MSI: MAPE=31.4% (N=109), OLI: MAPE=38.0% (N=74)]. The satisfactory agreement of Chl-a retrievals between the synchronous MSI and OLI images (N=2,293,821, MAPE=34.6%) supported the establishment of the virtual constellation. MSI- and OLI- derived Chl-a in nine major lakes in the studied area exhibited apparent seasonal variability from 2013 to 2022, particularly after 2017. Results highlight a solution to establish the Landsat/Sentinel-2 virtual constellation for improving the spatial and temporal resolutions of a database of lake water quality.

The forest area of South Kalimantan covers an area of 1,779,982 hectares contained in the Decree of the Minister of Forestry Number SK. 435/Menhut-II/2009, there is a Protected Forest Area in Liang Anggang District. Liang Anggang District has an area of approximately 8,586 hectares, while the protected forest area of Liang Anggang District is approximately 960 hectares. Changes in protected forest land cover in Liang Anggang District are seen with the help of Remote Sensing Technology and Geographic Information Systems (GIS). This study aims to analyze land cover change in Liang Anggang District, South Kalimantan, between 2018 and 2022 using the Maximum Likelihood Classification method with the help of Remote Sensing and Geographic Information Systems (GIS). The aim is to evaluate changes and carefully interpret land cover. A 960-hectare protected forest area in Liang Anggang sub-district was monitored using the Sentinel-2 satellite with a pixel thickness of 10 meters x 10 meters. The results showed a reduction in water bodies by 141 ha (1.64%), open land by 637 ha (7.42%), and forests by 562 ha (6.55%), while there was an increase in settlements (371 ha) and shrubs (969 ha). Accuracy analysis using confusion matrix shows an Overall Accuracy of 93.33%, indicating a high level of accuracy. This study highlights the importance of Remote Sensing and GIS technologies in monitoring and analyzing land cover change to support conservation policies and natural resource management in South Kalimantan

The article provides theoretical and methodological substantiation and a structural formulation of a holistic paradigm for sustainable land resource management in rural areas within the "twin transition" (digital and green) framework. The study proves that digitalization provides a high-precision instrumental toolkit for gathering, processing, and analyzing spatial data. At the same time, ecologization dictates the sustainable development trajectory by establishing critical environmental thresholds for anthropogenic loads on agroecosystems. The core role of the Comprehensive Spatial Development Plan of the Territorial Community (CSDP) formatted as File Geodatabases (GDB/GeoJSON) is conceptualized as the primary instrument for municipal spatial planning. The study establishes a three-tiered spatial data architecture for community land management, integrating base spatial layers (orthophotomaps and DEM), thematic environmental layers (soil variations, slope angles, water protection zones), and dynamic real-time data (remote sensing, UAVs, and IoT sensors). The paper systematizes the classification of digital tools (Sentinel-2, Landsat, SAR, LiDAR, Web-GIS), highlighting their practical applications in precision farming and erosion control. The paper formalizes a mathematical model for soil organic carbon (SOC) dynamics and presents an optimization objective to maximize the net eco-economic value of the community's land bank. The paper also elaborates specific protocols for eco-digital restoration of war-damaged lands (combining satellite analysis, bioremediation, and phytoremediation). Finally, an innovative organizational and economic mechanism is proposed that features dynamic rental rate adjustments based on soil quality metrics (ke), monetization of carbon farming credits, Payments for Ecosystem Services (PES), and blockchain-based smart contracts for land lease enforcement.

High-mountain lakes play a crucial role in mitigating climate impacts, regulating water flow, recharging groundwater, and ensuring ecological stability. Mapping their extent and monitoring changes is essential to prevent the loss of these ecosystems. However, research on monitoring high-mountain lakes is limited globally, and the subject has not received sufficient attention. This study utilized Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and remote sensing techniques to analyze changes in the surface area of ​​Boyuk Alagol between 1990 and 2023. The research employed the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) digital elevation model to generate slope and Topographic Wetness Index (TWI) maps, while Landsat 4-5 TM and Landsat 8 satellite imagery were used to calculate the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI), as well as to perform supervised classification for various years. Over the past thirty-three years, the lake lost 2.45% of its total surface area, corresponding to an annual reduction of 3.1 km². Research shows that GIS and remote sensing methods are effective for determining the boundaries, mapping, and assessing the dynamics of lakes and wetlands.

This study examines ocean conditions and rainfall-related flood candidates during Severe Tropical Storm Maysak using multisource observations in the northwestern South China Sea and Guangxi, China. Satellite products, atmospheric data, operational ocean products, published gauge summaries and official impact reports were analyzed with explicit observation windows and sensor provenance. Regional daily mean wind speed, significant wave height and mixed-layer depth peaked around 4 July 2026. Daily mean sea surface temperature (SST) on 5 July was 1.12 °C below the maximum during the study period. A daily first frontal analysis south of Hainan showed reductions of 15.3% in mean SST gradient and 25.6% in the mean daily strong front area between paired 15-day windows. Gradient decreases persisted across the tested windows and smoothing settings. Photosynthetically available radiation decreased by 24.1%, and diffuse attenuation at 490 nm increased by 7.9% across their respective windows. The merged chlorophyll-a retrievals increased descriptively by approximately 5.0%; sensor differences and limited common observations prevent interpreting this estimate as a bio-optical response independently corroborated across sensors. Integrated Multisatellite Retrievals for the Global Precipitation Measurement mission (IMERG) indicated a maximum accumulation of approximately 702 mm over the prolonged 2–16 July rainfall episode, including subsequent weather systems. Water-change masks identified 126.5 km2 of potential new inundation candidates, including 1.5 km2 of same-pixel multisensor overlap. The analysis documents marine changes, prolonged rainfall and regional water-change candidates within their stated observation windows.

Mostly any treaty or other form of agreement that State actors ratify is to secure the best interest for the people of the State. However, in the impact evaluation of such agreements, the human factor is often not accounted for. This thesis presents the study of such an agreement signed between Bangladesh and India, the Ganga Waters Treaty. This study marks a departure from existing rules and frameworks for the evaluation of transboundary river management and proposes that such evaluation should factor in the socio-economic indicators within its ambit under the principles of no significant harm which is a part of customary international water law. First, this study provides an outline of the history of how the Ganga Waters Treaty came into being. Second, it presents the results of socio-economic and remote sensing indicators achieved through difference-in-differences estimations. The riverbank regions along Ganga in Bangladesh is identified as the treatment region, the riverbank regions along the Brahmaputra in Bangladesh is the first control, and the second control group is the non-riverbank region along the Ganga. Although this thesis does not claim causality of its findings, it asks a pertinent question— whether bilateral treaties governing shared natural resources’ allocation, specifically river water, benefits the socio-economic conditions of downstream riparian communities? Proxies such as access to electricity and access to toilets are used to inform socio-economic variations across treatment and control groups. The findings reveal that predominantly, there is a positive and statistically significant relation of socio-economic indicators to the treatment effect. It also attempts to explain the differences in socio-economic factors across treatment and control regions with the help of satellite derived vegetation data. Overall, this thesis attempts to demystify the idea of a holistic evaluation of treaty outcomes for transboundary rivers, keeping the riparian communities at the center.

Aim: In Sierra Leone, the paucity of data on forest cover distribution and degradation limits the design and implementation of forest protection measures and the evaluation of the effectiveness of such measures. In view of the above, this study presents the first comparative analysis of district-level and forest reserve-level forest cover change in Sierra Leone, using a case study of the southern and eastern regions of the country. Study Design: A case-study research design and a remote-sensing approach using optical satellite imagery were adopted to quantify forest cover change at district and reserve levels over a 40-year interval. Place and Duration of Study: The study mapped and quantified forest cover change in Moyamba and Bo (Southern Region) and Kenema and Kailahun (Eastern Region) districts in 1986 and 2026. For each district, a forest reserve was identified and changes in its forest cover over the four decades were mapped and quantified. Methodology: Landsat imagery was acquired in 1986 (Landsat-5) and 2026 (Landsat-8). A simplified land-use land-cover (LULC) classification scheme was adopted, comprising six classes: forest, farm bush, grassland, mangrove, water body and others, to which the Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier was applied. Post-classification change detection was used to quantify LULC changes, and the corresponding district- and forest reserve-level statistics were summarised in bar charts. Accuracies were assessed using confusion matrices based on Google Earth imagery and ground-truth data for the 1986 and 2026 LULC maps, respectively. Results: The LULC classification achieved overall accuracies of 85.9% for the 1986 map and 96.6% for the 2026 map, and the higher accuracy recorded in the 2026 map is attributable to the improvement in radiometric resolution in Landsat-8 relative to Landsat-5. Forest declined across all districts, and a similar trend was recorded at the forest reserve level, except for Kangari in Bo, which recorded a slight increase of 1.4%. The decline in forest occurred in tandem with increases in either farm bush or grassland, or both. The overall decline in forest cover at the district level was greater (-35.2%) than that at the forest reserve level (-12.2%). Moyamba District, which is located along the Atlantic coast recorded a substantial decline (-28.6%) in mangrove. Conclusion: The lesser forest loss in forest reserves suggests a possible effect of protection measures. However, as unprotected forests decline, protected forests and mangroves would face increasing threats. Thus, there is a need to understand the dynamics of community forests, protected forests, and forest reserves. Moreover, studies are required of transboundary forest reserves, such as the Gola Forest, where cross-border differences in approaches and priorities have varying implications for forest management.

Abstract Climate change presents significant challenges to environmental sustainability, urban resilience, hydrological stability, and ecosystem health. Conventional climate vulnerability assessment approaches often rely on static, rule-based methods and isolated environmental indicators, limiting their ability to provide contextual and interpretable insights across geographically diverse regions. This paper proposes the Climate Risk Intelligence Index (CRII), an AI-augmented, satellite-based framework for assessing climate vulnerability across India. The framework integrates multiple Earth observation and climate datasets, including MODIS Land Surface Temperature (LST), MODIS Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL) built-up data, ERA5 rainfall reanalysis, and the JRC Global Surface Water dataset. These indicators are processed and aggregated into a composite climate vulnerability index across approximately 3,840 geospatial grid cells covering India. The framework also incorporates a Large Language Model (LLM)-based reasoning layer using the Groq API and the Llama 3.1 8B Instant model to support contextual environmental interpretation, dominant-risk identification, and interactive climate intelligence generation. Experimental analysis examines climate vulnerability patterns across flood-prone coastal regions, metropolitan areas, ecologically sensitive landscapes, and high-temperature arid regions. The AI reasoning component provides responses in approximately 1–3 seconds per query, supporting interactive environmental analysis. The proposed CRII framework demonstrates the potential of integrating satellite-based Earth observation, geospatial analytics, composite risk assessment, and AI-assisted reasoning into an interpretable climate decision-support system. The framework is intended to support climate vulnerability assessment, environmental monitoring, disaster preparedness, urban resilience analysis, and climate adaptation planning across India. Keywords Climate Risk Intelligence Index (CRII); Climate Vulnerability Assessment; Remote Sensing; Earth Observation; Artificial Intelligence; Large Language Models; Geospatial Analytics; Environmental Intelligence; Climate Risk; India.

Rare earth elements (REEs) are strategically critical materials indispensable to clean energy technology, defense systems, and consumer electronics. The United States currently imports the majority of REEs from China, creating a critical supply chain vulnerability that federal policy now mandates addressing through domestic sourcing. Appalachian coal mine drainage systems represent a significant but largely uncharacterized secondary REE source: regional surveys estimate 808 tons of REE production potential annually at $192 million contained value, with dissolved REE concentrations averaging 232.6 to 303.4 micrograms per liter in Central and Northern Appalachian basins respectively. Despite this economic and environmental significance, dissolved REE water chemistry in coal-associated acid mine drainage (AMD) systems remains poorly characterized in many regions, and the application of hyperspectral satellite remote sensing to AMD-dominated REE environments remains largely untested. This review synthesizes the state of knowledge across three converging fields: (1) the geological and geochemical controls on REE enrichment in coal-bearing strata and their mobilization into acid mine drainage, (2) the evolution of hyperspectral remote sensing instrumentation toward spaceborne REE detection, and (3) the methodological challenges of integrating geospatial and geochemical data for critical mineral assessment. Drawing on evidence from Appalachian, Chinese, and Russian coal basins, we identify five fundamental gaps in the current literature, most notably the absence, to our knowledge, of any published study linking coal-genetic models of rare earth elements and yttrium (REY) enrichment to the demonstrated capabilities and limitations of spaceborne hyperspectral detection in iron-dominated AMD settings. We argue that realizing the potential of remote sensing for AMD-REE characterization requires resolving a fundamental spectral challenge: the near-ubiquitous presence of iron oxyhydroxide precipitates, whose broad absorption features can mask the narrow diagnostic signatures of REEs. Kentucky's Wolf Creek Watershed, underlain by REE-enriched Pennsylvanian coal seams, is presented as one illustrative case where these questions could be addressed. This review concludes by outlining priority directions for future coupled geochemical-spectral research applicable to AMD systems across Appalachia and other coal-mining regions globally.

This archive provides the code, trained models, sample metadata, and evaluation results for the study "Extending Dynamic World Surface Water Mapping to Sentinel-1 with AlphaEarth Embeddings" (Mukherjee et al., submitted to IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Letters, preprint arXiv:2610.06704). OverviewThe models map surface water from Sentinel-1 SAR imagery. They are trained only on the Dynamic World water class (label band, class 0), with no task-specific manual labels. The main model combines Sentinel-1 VV, VH, and incidence angle with the 64-band AlphaEarth Foundations annual embedding, which is projected to 16 channels by a learned 1×1 convolution, in a ResNet34 U-Net. On 53 globally distributed scenes with 3 m PlanetScope-based reference maps, the model reaches a pooled water IoU of 0.85, compared with 0.77 for the Sentinel-1-only model and 0.75 for OPERA DSWx-S1. On 15 S1S2-Water test scenes it reaches 0.94, compared with 0.87 for OPERA DSWx-S1 (threshold 0.30). Trained models (trained_models/)- Main model, Sentinel-1 + acquisition-year AlphaEarth embeddings (ResNet34 U-Net with a 16-channel embedding bottleneck)- Sentinel-1-only comparison model with the same architecture, training split, and schedule- Sentinel-1 + previous-year AlphaEarth model, for use when acquisition-year embeddings are not yet availableEach model is packaged with its PyTorch/fastai checkpoint, per-band normalization statistics (band_stats.npz), validation threshold sweep, and evaluation summary. A model card, SHA-256 checksums, and MODEL_INFO.json describe inputs, band order, thresholds, and results. Code (source/)- Training (src/train.py), tiled inference with four-flip test-time augmentation and georeferenced probability outputs (src/infer.py), and evaluation (src/evaluate.py)- Scripts for sampling training sites, pairing Sentinel-1 with Dynamic World, retrieving AlphaEarth embeddings, and rebuilding training samples from public inputs- Evaluation workflows for the 53 PlanetScope-based scenes and the S1S2-Water benchmark, including OPERA DSWx-S1 processing, matched-resolution rescoring, and WorldCover error analysis- HPC (SLURM) job scripts, tests, requirements, and a data-preparation guide (examples/prepare_data.md) Sample metadata (source/metadata/)- Location, Sentinel-1 date, AlphaEarth year, train/validation split, and sampling source for all 5278 training tiles (4222 training, 1056 validation), as CSV and GeoJSON- Sentinel-1 scene identifiers, acquisition times, and reference-to-Sentinel-1 time offsets for the 53 evaluation scenes Results (source/results/)Per-scene and pooled metrics behind the tables and figures of the paper and its supplement, including sensitivity analyses, threshold sweeps, S1S2-Water results, and the OPERA DSWx-S1 comparison. Not includedSource satellite imagery, training raster tiles, and reference raster datasets are not redistributed. They can be rebuilt from public sources (Sentinel-1 GRD and Dynamic World via Google Earth Engine, and AlphaEarth Foundations embeddings via Source Cooperative) using the provided scripts and metadata. Licenses and attributionCode and models are released under the Apache License 2.0. Input data remain under their own terms. AlphaEarth Foundations Satellite Embedding and Dynamic World are CC BY 4.0, and Sentinel-1 data are subject to the Copernicus Sentinel Data Legal Notice. See THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. Related resourcesSource code: https://github.com/Rohit18/surfaceWaterMappingGlobal (v1.0)Models: https://huggingface.co/rohitm9/surfaceWaterGlobal (tag v2-labelclass)

Abstract The construction of dam in any region is economically helpful as it provides benefits in irrigation, hydel power generation, flood control and domestic water supply. However, the dam may bring significant land use changes that may influence vegetation condition and overall watershed sustainability which requires precise evaluation and monitoring. Remote sensing and GIS play a significant role in monitoring such spatial and temporal changes. The present study aims to assess the temporal dynamics of land use pattern and evaluate vegetation health the study area. The land use land cover classification is carried out by using Landsat satellite images with the help of supervised classification in GIS environment. NDVI, EVI and NDMI has been used for vegetation health assessment. The study has identified changes in land use land cover categories and spatial variations in vegetation density, conditions and moisture status. The study can help in sustainable land resource planning, vegetation conservation and watershed management in Salaulim Dam Watershed.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming agriculture through the integration of machine learning, deep learning, Internet of Things (IoT), remote sensing, robotics and data analytics. These technologies enable agricultural systems to process information from satellites, unmanned aerial vehicles, field sensors, weather stations, farm machinery and historical records to support timely and site-specific decisions. Current applications include crop-yield forecasting, disease and pest identification, weed detection, precision irrigation, soil and nutrient assessment, crop monitoring, harvesting, food-quality evaluation and supply-chain management. AI can improve the efficiency of water, fertilizer, pesticides and labour while supporting climate-resilient and sustainable production. Nevertheless, adoption is affected by data quality, infrastructure costs, connectivity, digital literacy, privacy, cyber security, interoperability and limited model interpretability. These issues are particularly important for smallholder farmers and regions with limited digital infrastructure. Future agricultural AI will increasingly combine IoT, remote sensing, edge computing, robotics, explainable AI and multimodal data. Successful implementation will require affordable technologies, reliable local datasets, farmer participation, responsible data governance and collaboration between agricultural and technological disciplines. AI should therefore be regarded as a decision-support and automation technology that complements, rather than replaces, agronomic knowledge and farmer experience.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly used to monitor environmental conditions, estimate exposures, and support health-related decision making. Yet the settings with substantial environmental-health burdens often have the least complete, representative, and accessible data. This narrative review examines three interconnected constraints (data quality, data bias, and data scarcity) and considers how they affect the reliability, generalisability, fairness, and practical usefulness of AI for environmental health in low-resource regions. The review synthesises 38 sources published between 2018 and 2025 covering air-quality sensing, water-quality prediction, satellite remote sensing, environmental exposure estimation, public-health surveillance, and algorithmic fairness. Across the literature, low-cost sensors can expand spatial coverage but require calibration and maintenance; monitoring and health records may under-represent exposed populations; and models developed elsewhere may transfer poorly without local validation. The review develops an integrated challenge–solution taxonomy linking each data limitation to its consequences for AI, technical mitigation strategies, and policy or community interventions. Case studies from India, Ethiopia, Uganda, and Ghana illustrate how these constraints interact in practice. The review identifies priorities for low-resource settings: shared benchmarks, local and subgroup validation, explicit uncertainty reporting, interoperable data systems, stronger environmental and health surveillance, and governance arrangements that enable responsible use of local data. The central implication is that AI can extend environmental-health monitoring, but technical innovation cannot fully substitute for representative local measurements and health data.

Mediterranean forests are currently among the ecosystems most vulnerable to climate change and mounting anthropogenic pressures. The increasing frequency and severity of droughts, coupled with the intensive overexploitation of forest resources—through overgrazing, quarrying, illegal logging, and urban expansion—are exacerbating the structural and functional degradation of these natural environments. Extensive research across the Mediterranean basin indicates that chronic water stress triggers a gradual decline in biomass, elevated tree mortality, and forest canopy fragmentation, directly compromising ecosystem resilience. Consequently, the spatio-temporal monitoring of vegetation dynamics has become a critical scientific and practical imperative to understand degradation trajectories and inform sustainable management strategies. Satellite remote sensing serves as a primary tool for analyzing forest cover shifts across various scales, utilizing spectral vegetation indices like the Modified Soil Adjusted Vegetation Index (MSAVI). This index is widely applied to evaluate plant vigor and biomass dynamics, particularly in semi-arid regions where the influence of bare soil is substantial.

(English) The impact of livestock farming on soil degradation has been widely discussed, with cattle production being attributed a significant impact both globally and locally. This research, entitled "Management model for the restoration of land used for livestock farming in the department of Córdoba, Colombia. A contribution of regenerative livestock farming to the sustainable development of the territory - Comparative case studies," analyzes the evolution of regenerative livestock farming, especially in Latin America, and adapts a methodology to evaluate the efficiency of this model on the soil using biological and spatial indicators, comparing it with a conventional model on farms in Córdoba. It also evaluates the contribution of these models to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and proposes a conceptual model for the sustainable management and restoration of livestock soils. An analysis was carried out on the progress of regenerative livestock farming worldwide and in Latin America, finding a significant increase in its adoption since 2018, especially in 2019, when the preservation of biodiversity, water, and soil health began to be valued. Macro indicators of soil condition were defined and 12 farms were selected to analyze conventional and regenerative production models. Edaphic macro and mesofauna were evaluated, satellite images were analyzed, and information on vegetation cover was collected, using biological and spatial indicators to measure the restorative capacity of the models. A SWOT (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats) analysis was also conducted, concluding that the regenerative model is more efficient in grazing practices, profitability, and biodiversity, allowing for passive restoration of the ecosystem. A methodology was developed to analyze the efficiency of regenerative livestock farming, establishing methods for collecting biotic and spatial data, which facilitates continuous soil diagnosis and monitoring. The study area, the duration of the analysis, the phases of the process, the indicators, and the multitemporal analysis of the plant component were defined using remote sensing and GIS technologies, providing the necessary data for a detailed analysis. It was concluded that regenerative livestock farming is an economical and sustainable low-cost model that improves productivity without agrochemicals and prevents erosion, promoting soil restoration through sustainable practices. This model also contributes to the fulfillment of the SDGs, especially in food security, climate action, and ecosystem restoration, promoting greater biological biodiversity and vegetation cover in the study areas. The results show a positive impact on soil health, vegetation development, and macrofauna, with notable root growth and no degraded soils. Regenerative livestock farming works in harmony with nature, improving the living conditions and health of livestock. Regenerative livestock farming is presented as a key tool for addressing the environmental, social, and productive challenges of livestock farming, restoring soils and ecosystems, and reversing the damage caused by overgrazing and the use of agrochemicals in conventional models. It restores soil fertility, promotes a natural cycle of regeneration, and facilitates the recovery of native species of flora and fauna, increasing the ecosystem's resistance to external disturbances. In terms of species abundance, a total of 763 individuals were quantified between both systems, distributed across 19 taxonomic orders, with 630 individuals in the regenerative model and 133 in the conventional model. The Shannon-Wiener Index (H') under the regenerative model was 2.06, reflecting high biological diversity and efficiency in restoration and long-term sustainability. (Català) S'ha discutit àmpliament la incidència de la ramaderia en la deterioració del sòl, atribuint-se a la producció bovina un impacte significatiu tant a nivell mundial com local. Aquesta recerca, titulada “Model de gestió per a la restauració del sòl dedicat a l'activitat ramadera en el departament de Còrdova, Colòmbia. Una aportació de la ramaderia regenerativa al desenvolupament sostenible del territori - Estudis de casos comparatius”, analitza l'evolució de la ramaderia regenerativa, especialment a Amèrica Llatina, i adapta una metodologia per a avaluar l'eficiència d'aquest model sobre el sòl mitjançant indicadors biològics i espacials, comparant amb un model convencional en finques de Còrdova. També avalua la contribució d'aquests models als Objectius de Desenvolupament Sostenible (ODS) i proposa un model conceptual per a la gestió i restauració sostenible de sòls ramaders. Es va realitzar una anàlisi sobre l'avanç de la ramaderia regenerativa a nivell mundial i a Amèrica Llatina, trobant un augment significatiu en la seva adopció des de 2018, especialment en 2019, quan es va començar a valorar la preservació de la biodiversitat, l'aigua i la salut del sòl. Es van definir macroindicadors de l'estat del sòl i es van seleccionar 12 finques per a analitzar els models de producció convencional i regeneratiu. Es va avaluar la macro i mesofauna edàfica, es van analitzar imatges satel·litàries i es va recopilar informació sobre la cobertura vegetal, utilitzant indicadors biològics i espacials per a mesurar la capacitat restaurativa dels models. També es va realitzar una anàlisi DOFA (Febleses, Oportunitats, Fortaleses i Amenaces), concloent que el model regeneratiu és més eficient en pràctiques de pasturatge, rendibilitat i biodiversitat, permetent una restauració passiva de l'ecosistema. Es va desenvolupar una metodologia per a analitzar l'eficiència de la ramaderia regenerativa, establint mètodes per a recol·lectar dades biòtiques i espacials, la qual cosa facilita un diagnòstic i monitoratge continu del sòl. Es van definir l'àrea d'estudi, la durada de l'anàlisi, les fases del procés, els indicadors i l'anàlisi multitemporal del component vegetal mitjançant tecnologies de teledetecció i SIG, proporcionant les dades necessàries per a una anàlisi detallada. Es va concloure que la ramaderia regenerativa és un model econòmic i sostenible amb baix cost, que millora la productivitat sense agroquímics i evita processos erosius, promovent la restauració de sòls mitjançant pràctiques sostenibles. Aquest model també contribueix al compliment dels ODS, especialment en seguretat alimentària, acció climàtica i restauració d'ecosistemes, promovent major biodiversitat biològica i cobertura vegetal en les zones d'estudi. Els resultats mostren un impacte positiu en la salut del sòl, el desenvolupament de la vegetació i la macrofauna, amb un creixement notable d'arrels i absència de sòls degradats. La ramaderia regenerativa treballa en harmonia amb la naturalesa, millorant les condicions de vida i salut del bestiar. La ramaderia regenerativa es presenta com una eina clau per a enfrontar els desafiaments ambientals, socials i productius de la ramaderia, restaurant sòls i ecosistemes, revertint el mal causat per la sobrepastura i l'ús d'agroquímics en els models convencionals. Recupera la fertilitat del sòl, promou un cicle natural de regeneració i facilita la recuperació d'espècies natives de flora i fauna, augmentant la resistència de l'ecosistema enfront de pertorbacions externes. En relació a l'abundància d'espècies, es van quantificar 763 individus en total entre tots dos sistemes, distribuïts en 19 ordres taxonòmics, amb 630 individus en el model regeneratiu i 133 en el convencional. L'Índex de Shannon-*Wiener (H') sota el model regeneratiu va ser de 2,06, la qual cosa reflecteix una alta diversitat biològica i eficiència en la restauració i sostenibilitat a llarg termini. (Español) Se ha discutido ampliamente la incidencia de la ganadería en el deterioro del suelo, atribuyéndose a la producción bovina un impacto significativo tanto a nivel mundial como local. Esta investigación, titulada “Modelo de gestión para la restauración del suelo dedicado a la actividad ganadera en el departamento de Córdoba, Colombia. Un aporte de la ganadería regenerativa al desarrollo sostenible del territorio - Estudios de casos comparativos”, analiza la evolución de la ganadería regenerativa, especialmente en América Latina, y adapta una metodología para evaluar la eficiencia de este modelo sobre el suelo mediante indicadores biológicos y espaciales, comparando con un modelo convencional en fincas de Córdoba. También evalúa la contribución de estos modelos a los Objetivos de Desarrollo Sostenible (ODS) y propone un modelo conceptual para la gestión y restauración sostenible de suelos ganaderos. Se realizó un análisis sobre el avance de la ganadería regenerativa a nivel mundial y en América Latina, encontrando un aumento significativo en su adopción desde 2018, especialmente en 2019, cuando se empezó a valorar la preservación de la biodiversidad, el agua y la salud del suelo. Se definieron macroindicadores del estado del suelo y se seleccionaron 12 fincas para analizar los modelos de producción convencional y regenerativo. Se evaluó la macro y mesofauna edáfica, se analizaron imágenes satelitales y se recopiló información sobre la cobertura vegetal, utilizando indicadores biológicos y espaciales para medir la capacidad restaurativa de los modelos. También se realizó un análisis DOFA (Debilidades, Oportunidades, Fortalezas y Amenazas), concluyendo que el modelo regenerativo es más eficiente en prácticas de pastoreo, rentabilidad y biodiversidad, permitiendo una restauración pasiva del ecosistema. Se desarrolló una metodología para analizar la eficiencia de la ganadería regenerativa, estableciendo métodos para recolectar datos bióticos y espaciales, lo que facilita un diagnóstico y monitoreo continuo del suelo.
