The aim of this article is to utilize remote sensing in the bathymetricstudy of a river section, by integrating GIS into 3D modeling of theseabed in order to measure, map, and assess sediment accumulation forpotential exploitation of sandbanks.This work is part of a broader effort to modernize the exploitationof this resource, which until now has been carried out without planningand control tools. A methodological approach combining passiveand active methods was adopted. The passive approach relied on theanalysis of satellite imagery, particularly NDWI ( Normalized DataWave Index) data. Difference Water Index) and infrared (IR) imagingwere used to identify wetlands, depositional environments, and riverdynamics. In addition, an active approach employed a GT52 echosounder to collect precise bathymetric data on the riverbed depth. Thisdata was then processed in a GIS environment to generate a DigitalTerrain Model (DTM), a depth interpolation, and a 3D model of theriver cross-section. The results enabled the identification of the maindepositional areas of exploitable sandbanks and their volume, the assessmentof their accessibility, and the proposal of an optimized extractionplan. This work thus provides a reliable technical basis for guidingindustrial sand extraction with a focus on ecological sustainability andalso serves as a decision-making tool for this economic sector.

Agricultural production in Africa’s semi-arid tropics is increasingly constrained by erratic rainfall, recurrent droughts, soil degradation and mounting climate variability, threatening food security, rural livelihoods and ecosystem stability. This chapter critically examines the role of intelligent irrigation systems and advanced soil diagnostics as transformative pathways for climate-smart agriculture in the region. Intelligent irrigation, including sensor-based scheduling, automated drip systems and satellite-guided water management, enables precise water application, reduces waste, enhances crop productivity and builds drought resilience. Innovations in soil diagnostics, such as portable spectrometry, remote sensing and machine-learning–enabled nutrient mapping, provide real-time insights into soil health, optimizing input use efficiency and minimizing environmental impacts. Drawing on global experiences from Brazil, India and Israel, as well as African initiatives in Kenya, Niger and Zimbabwe, the chapter situates these technologies within institutional, socio-economic and infrastructural contexts. Emphasis is placed on affordability, farmer capacity and policy support to ensure equitable adoption, particularly among smallholder farmers. The main topics covered in the chapter are (i) climate challenges and vulnerability in semi-arid African agriculture, (ii) intelligent irrigation technologies and water-use optimization, (iii) advanced soil diagnostics and nutrient management innovations, (iv) institutional, policy and socio-economic factors affecting adoption, and (v) global lessons and African case studies for scalable climate-smart agriculture. The chapter demonstrates how innovations can enhance resilience, productivity and sustainability, offering research, investment and policy priorities to scale climate-smart agriculture across Africa.

Fluvial deposits with a robust chrono-stratigraphy can be used to establish the history of river morpho-dynamics and their relationship with paleoclimate. Quaternary climate change has impacted temperature, precipitation and sea-level, as well as land cover, and so is likely also to have impacted river flows and sediment yield. At such timescales, tectonic influences may also be important. Yet Quaternary landscape evolution in tropical river environments, such as Indonesia, remains poorly known, especially over Middle to Late Pleistocene and Holocene timescales. In this context, the focus of this thesis is the Kampar Kanan River, a meandering tropical river in Sumatra Island, Indonesia, that has a gentle slope, sand-gravel beds and bends that migrated laterally due to bank erosion. The aim of the thesis is to quantify how late Quaternary climate change impacted river morpho-dynamics in the Kampar Kanan River, with particular attention to the role of tectonic forcing as an additional control on fluvial behaviour. This study uses both a chrono-stratigraphic framework and fluvial modelling. Satellite images show the recent geometry of the river and combining remote sensing with field observations allowed current river dynamics to be established and links to tectonic history to be made. Sedimentological analysis, utilizing X-ray diffraction and granulometry, was used to investigate facies changes and associated paleoenvironments. This was supported by luminescence dating to provide dates for certain facies and hence to link fluvial morpho-dynamics to known Quaternary climatic histories. To obtain the lateral distribution of channel migration and erosion needed to understand fluvial behaviour, simulation of fluvial dynamics was conducted using a numerical model (eRiDynas model) of water flow and sediment transport to develop a deeper understanding of the drivers of morpho-dynamics. Conceptual scenarios of how climate change impacted the relative balance between monsoon and sediment supply were applied to the model to quantify how it impacted fluvial morpho-dynamics. Results of sedimentological and luminescence dating analyses showed that sedimentation of the Kampar River occurred in the Upper Middle Pleistocene with the presence of massive gravelly channel deposits. This happened in a period of high global glacier cover, cold conditions and low sea levels at Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 6 or earlier, possibly suggesting a significant increase in sediment supply and/or reduction in sediment transport capacity due to drier conditions. A hiatus in the sedimentary record suggested that sedimentation reduced substantially, and intensive erosion and tectonic activities (particularly uplifting) occurred during glacial to interglacial periods between MIS-4 and 3. In the Late Pleistocene, fining-upward sandy gravels were deposited at late MIS-3, and the river became more associated with low amplitude point bars reflected in lateral accretion deposits. Overbank formations were deposited, indicating the onset of large-scale floodplain inundation and more intensive bend growth, driven primarily by tectonic uplift and reduced fluvial discharge rather than increased humidity, a pattern that continued into the Holocene. This evidence suggested that fluvial morpho-dynamics were primarily climate-controlled, whilst tectonic forcing, particularly uplifting, acted as an additional significant control on sedimentation and terrace development. Numerical modelling further confirmed these findings: decreasing water discharge, representative of drier glacial conditions, and increasing flow discharge, representative of interglacial conditions, produced contrasting river behaviours in terms of sediment deposition, erosion rates, inundation area formation, and bar development, with tectonic uplift amplifying these differences particularly in the southern floodplain. Tectonic forcing therefore exerted a substantial influence on these dynamics, highlighting the importance of accounting for both climatic and tectonic controls in tropical fluvial systems.

Environmental monitoring and natural resource management have become increasingly complex due to rapid climate change, population growth, industrial development, and increasing pressure on ecosystems. Traditional environmental assessment methods often require extensive human resources, time-consuming field surveys, and large financial investments. The emergence of machine learning has introduced advanced computational approaches that improve the accuracy, efficiency, and scalability of environmental analysis. Machine learning algorithms can process large volumes of environmental data collected through satellites, remote sensing systems, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, sensors, and geographic information systems to identify patterns, predict environmental changes, and support sustainable decision-making. This research explores the applications of machine learning in environmental monitoring and natural resource management by examining its role in climate analysis, biodiversity conservation, water resource management, agricultural sustainability, pollution detection, and ecosystem assessment. Machine learning models such as artificial neural networks, random forests, support vector machines, and deep learning techniques have demonstrated significant potential in predicting environmental risks and optimizing resource utilization. These technologies enable real-time monitoring of environmental conditions and provide valuable insights for policymakers, researchers, and environmental managers. The study also discusses challenges associated with machine learning adoption, including data availability, computational requirements, algorithm transparency, and ethical considerations. The integration of artificial intelligence with environmental science provides new opportunities for developing sustainable strategies and improving responses to environmental challenges. The findings highlight that machine learning can serve as a powerful tool for achieving efficient natural resource management and supporting global environmental sustainability goals.

HistoryChlorophyll-a (Chl-a) is a key indicator of phytoplankton biomass and trophic conditions in freshwater ecosystems.This study integrated field measurements and satellite observations to evaluate and refine empirical approaches for estimating Chl-a concentrations in the Karatomar and Verkhnetobol reservoirs using Sentinel-2 imagery, the Normalized Difference Chlorophyll Index (NDCI), and spectral reflectance data.The total water-surface area investigated was 181.1 km², comprising 93.7 km² of the Karatomar Reservoir and 87.4 km² of the Verkhnetobol Reservoir.From April to October 2024, Chl-a concentrations were determined using standardized laboratory methods and integrated with satellite-derived estimates to improve retrieval accuracy.Reservoir-specific relationships between remotely sensed spectral variables and measured Chl-a concentrations were established, and second-order polynomial equations were derived for quantitative Chl-a estimation.The optimized approach was subsequently applied to Sentinel-2 observations from 2019-2024 to characterize the spatial and temporal dynamics of Chl-a in both reservoirs.In 2024, as well as during May of 2019-2023, mean Chl-a concentrations in both reservoirs remained below 30 µg L⁻¹, corresponding to the ecological category "Relatively satisfactory situation."However, localized areas of the Karatomar Reservoir exhibited Chl-a concentrations exceeding 50 µg L⁻¹ during July-September of 2019, 2020, 2021, and 2023, indicating severe ecological deterioration ("Environmental disaster") and the occurrence of intense algal blooms.Similarly, although mean Chl-a concentrations in the Verkhnetobol Reservoir remained below 30 µg L⁻¹ throughout 2019-2024, localized concentrations above 50 µg L⁻¹ were detected in September 2020, 2021, and 2023 and were associated with intensive algal proliferation.Elevated Chl-a concentrations were particularly evident during years characterized by reduced spring snowmelt inflow and declining reservoir water levels.Spatially, Chl-a hotspots occurred predominantly in littoral areas and zones of dense aquatic vegetation, including macrophyte-dominated habitats.Overall, the integration of standardized laboratory measurements with Sentinel-2-derived spectral information provides an effective approach for reconstructing and monitoring spatiotemporal patterns of Chl-a and identifying areas susceptible to algal blooms in large freshwater reservoirs.

The Lower Diyala region has played a central role in discussions on the relationship between complex societies and large-scale irri-gation systems in Mesopotamia. Since Robert McC. Adams’ surveys in the 1950s, his reconstruction of irrigation networks has remained the main point of reference for the region and a staple of our discipline. This study revisits Adams’ original survey data within the framework of the Floodplain Project (University of Bologna, dir. N. Marchetti). By combining his field observations with declassified CORONA imagery and multi-temporal satellite data, we corrected several spatial distortions in the original maps. This work identified a number of previously undocumented archaeological sites and hydraulic features. This revised spatial framework allows a closer alignment between irrigation layouts and local topography, offering a more robust basis for chronological interpretation. Adopting a longue durée perspective, the paper reassesses patterns of water management from the early historical periods to the Islamic era. The results highlight both long-term continuities and significant reorganizations of irrigation systems in response to changing political contexts and environmental conditions. More broadly, this contribution illustrates the value of reprocessing legacy datasets using methodological innovation to refine our understanding of ancient hydraulic landscapes in Mesopotamia.

Satellite altimetry provides near-global observations for recovering the marine gravity field, but conventional nadir altimetry has limited capability to resolve short-wavelength features, particularly in coastal and sediment-covered marine basins. The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission offers a new opportunity to improve marine gravity recovery through wide-swath, high-precision measurements of sea surface height. Here, we use 1.5 years of SWOT observations to derive gravity anomalies and vertical gravity gradients across the Gulf of Mexico. Comparison with independent shipborne gravity data indicates an effective spatial resolution of approximately 10 km and an approximately 8% lower root-mean-square deviation than the SIO V32.1 multi-mission altimetry gravity model, with larger relative improvements in a dynamically active region near the Loop Current. SWOT-derived vertical gravity gradients sharpen the expression of known tectonic elements, including extinct spreading ridge segments, fracture zones, outer marginal troughs, basement step-ups, and salt-basin architecture. They also delineate tectonic fabrics that are poorly resolved in conventional gravity products and not clearly expressed in bathymetry, including linear structures near the Chicxulub impact crater and gravitationally detached foldbelts buried beneath thick sediments. Interpreted together with existing seismic, aeromagnetic, drilling, and geological constraints, these observations provide independent information on the opening and passive-margin evolution of the Gulf of Mexico. Our results show that SWOT-derived marine gravity can extend wide-swath altimetry beyond oceanographic applications and provide a remote-sensing approach for investigating sediment-covered tectonic structures in marine basins.

Globalization has accelerated social, economic, technological, and political growth of countries. On the contrary, it also results in intensifying pollution, increasing ecological footprint, and eventually changing the global climate. Monitoring the changes in the key environmental components is crucial for tracking environmental processes, ensuring the safety of the overall environment along with public health through sustainable management/planning leading to sustainable development. Monitoring environmental pollution in the traditional way/method is not significant and is also time-consuming. And it has become important to have updated information and reliable data on environmental components and changes occurring in them. Thus, sensors are the most precise, reliable, easy-handling, and cost/labor-effective technology for real-time monitoring of environmental components. These devices detect various environmental situations like radiation, heat, moisture, pressure, 38 temperature, GHG concentration, and so forth, and convert them into a human-understandable form with colorful illustrations. These sensors are wired, wireless, stationary, or mobile in structure and function. Recently, wireless and Internet of Things (IoT) based sensors are widely used for smart monitoring of environmental factors like air, Green House Gases (GHGs), land, soil, freshwater, marine environment, forest, biodiversity, and so forth, and analyzed through machine learning (ML) techniques. Remote Sensing based high-resolution satellite/ground-based techniques/ imageries in association with GIS tools are also used to monitor various environmental factors like air pollution, earth's surface temperature, surface and groundwater/wastewater monitoring, vegetation changes, marine monitoring, geological disasters, weather phenomena, glacial snow melt, and climate change, and so forth. Laboratory-based sensor technologies like trace-metal sensors, radioisotope sensors, volatile organic compound sensors, and biological sensors are utilized for monitoring environmental contaminants in drinking water, stormwater, pretreatment of wastewater, and ambient air quality. Therefore, this chapter will discuss the use of modern developed sensor technologies and techniques for monitoring environmental issues, particularly focusing on pollution, climate change, and other environmental degradation factors. Thus, this chapter is an overview of available sensor technologies used for monitoring environmental components.

Cyanobacterial blooms are a direct manifestation of lake eutrophication. Accurately obtaining their spatial distribution is of great significance for lake ecological monitoring and governance. Using screened Sentinel‑2 L2A multispectral satellite imagery, this dataset addresses complex inland‑water interferences over Dianchi Lake. SMBWI water‑index and morphological filtering are adopted to construct high‑precision water masks. Taking the S2_AI cyanobacteria index as core indicator and false‑color infrared composite as visual reference, cyanobacterial bloom extents are determined via density slicing, and pseudo‑mask labels are generated with manual calibration. Processed from 22 cloud‑free valid scenes, the dataset covers bloom‑prone periods of Dianchi Lake from 2017 to 2024at 10 m spatial resolution. It includes three types of GeoTIFF tile products: 5‑band derived imagery, cyanobacteria index layers and binary pseudo‑masks of cyanobacterial blooms. Forty‑eight manually‑annotated tiles are used for quality validation. For heavy‑bloom scenes, mean IoU reaches 0.9654 with Precision=1.0; for low‑concentration fragmented bloom scenes IoU decreases while Precision remains 1.0, showing nearly zero false positives and mainly omission errors. Tiles and corresponding labels are one‑to‑one matched. The dataset can support remote‑sensing algorithm development, deep‑learning model training and long‑term dynamic analysis for cyanobacterial‑bloom monitoring over Dianchi Lake.

Floods remain one of the most frequent and destructive natural hazards, causing severe loss of life, infrastructure damage, and economic disruption across the globe. Conventional monitoring approaches that depend on river gauges, rainfall stations, and manual field surveys suffer from restricted spatial coverage, delayed analysis, and heavy reliance on human intervention, which often results in late detection and slow emergency response. This work presents a real-time flood monitoring and alert framework that fuses satellite/aerial remote-sensing imagery with a SegNet-based convolutional neural network to perform pixel-level semantic segmentation of flooded and non-flooded regions. The segmentation output is combined with auxiliary environmental parameters, namely rainfall intensity and river water level, to compute a quantitative flood-coverage percentage and to classify the overall risk into Safe, Moderate, or Very High categories. The framework is delivered through a Flask-based web application that allows users to upload imagery, view segmentation overlays and heat-maps, receive real-time alerts, and download automatically generated PDF reports. Experimental evaluation on annotated flood-imagery datasets shows a mean pixel accuracy of 95.2%, a mean Intersection-over-Union of 91.7%, and a Dice coefficient of 92.5%, together with a mean per-image inference latency below two seconds. These results indicate that the proposed system offers faster, more accurate, and more scalable flood detection than traditional ground-based techniques, making it a practical tool for disaster-management authorities.

Optical Earth observation satellites provide scientists and coastal managers with multiple information on the seafloor, water column, environmental parameters, natural or human-induced pressures, ecosystem services or biodiversity. However, the use of remote sensing is strongly constrained by the presence of liquid water which attenuates the light signal depending on the wavelength and depth. All applications that require perceiving the bottom through the water column, such as habitat mapping and bathymetry estimation are thus affected by a limit of about 20 m beyond which the light signal becomes too weak and noisy to provide accurate information. This study uses hypertemporal (HT) data cubes constituted by long time series of optical images from the Sentinel-2 satellites to improve data quality and significantly extend this commonly accepted limit to depths reaching 70 to 80 m. The generated multi-temporal composite images reveal details of the seabed in remote areas of the world's oceans, never before perceived from space. Satellite-derived bathymetric (SDB) estimates using this new data layers and Random Forest and XGBoost machine learning algorithms show very good correlations with reference data over the extended depth range at 100 m spatial resolution. At the study sites located in the Mediterranean Sea as well as in the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans, where the waters are clearest, good estimates were obtained across the entire 0-80 m bathymetric range, with Mean Absolute Errors (MAE) of 3.21 m in Martinique, 2.62 m in Corsica, 1.88 m in La Reunion, and 3.17 m in New Caledonia. The two more turbid sites in the North Atlantic also maintained low MAE levels, even when the bottom signal was no longer visible, thanks to the water column properties information provided by the HT images: 4.74 m in Ouessant and 2.10 m in Glenan. Analyses of cloud cover, time series length, temporal statistics, geographical areas and water types specify the influence of these parameters on data quality as well as the limits of application of the models. The processing chains developed here, using freely accessible Sentinel-2 satellite data available worldwide, enables operational implementation for fast and large-scale data production.

During his trip to the Antarctic in the 1997/8 summer season, English composer Peter Maxwell Davies (1934–2016) was struck by the sights and sounds of the icy landscape. As he crossed the Drake Passage on the RRS James Clark Ross, he spoke about the intensity of the experience of being in the pack ice as the ship approached the islands. He particularly emphasized “the emptiness, the whiteness, the purity of the air, the sound of silence, the physical impact of the ship crashing the ice as it goes through the soles of your feet, right into your brain” (Davies, DF 61.B4, 04:11:32–04:14:10). This statement is just one example that demonstrates the effect that Davies’s time in the Antarctic had on him; his trip ultimately led to a published version of his Antarctic diary and five compositions, most notably the Antarctic Symphony (2000).1 These musical depictions of the Antarctic were affected by the external agendas that shaped his time in the region, as were his written and documentary comments about his experiences. Scholarship about Davies’s Antarctic visit and his resulting musical output is limited. Though the trip and symphony were commissioned by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) as a way of increasing public investment in their activities, the circumstances that led to the project have not been fully considered, nor has the visit’s impact on Davies. Drawing on ecocriticism, environmental history, and environmental studies, I use Davies’s Antarctic Symphony as a case study to argue that sonic depictions of landscapes have been and still are colored by imperial and neo-imperial agendas such as those explicated by environmental historian Adrian Howkins in Frozen Empires (2017). The changes that Davies observed in the Antarctic played an important role in his own considerations of the region, its history, and its future, and these all appeared in his writings (musical and otherwise). Davies’s trip was spent on islands that are significant to British Antarctic history. Additionally, because the region is historically uninhabited, the effects of elements that shape it (such as exploration, international governance, and climate change) are more evident than in places with a longer record of human influence. The relatively abbreviated history of human impact in the Antarctic enables considerations of its real and imagined landscapes and sonic engagements with environmental disruption to be mapped onto other parts of the globe, as similar approaches can be seen in the treatment of other places that are often part of the same imperial network.2 Davies’s symphony provides a useful Antarctic case study because of how he incorporated the region’s history and ecology into the work. The Antarctic region has been a source of fascination for the British since the eighteenth century. Because of its promise of wealth in the form of whaling and sealing and the uncertainty surrounding then-hypothetical land, explorers sought resources and territory that had not yet been claimed by other European colonial powers. Both before and after the continent’s official discovery in 1820, the polar and sub-polar south attracted explorers who saw their expeditions to the region and its islands as a means of securing their own reputations or, in the case of whalers, their fortunes.3 The Antarctic has since continued to be important for commercial and geopolitical exploits, and it has proven to be culturally compelling in art, literature, and music.4 The people (primarily men) who have explored the larger region have been venerated for their scientific discoveries, supposed heroic exploits, and embodiment of British cultural values.5 British activity in the region in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries encouraged expeditions that furthered agendas related to whaling and territorial expansion (like those of James Cook and James Clark Ross). As Antarctic historian Ben Maddison demonstrates, this focus was because interest in the southern region was driven more by motives of acquisition rather than inquisition, meaning that scientific pursuits were much less of a priority than those that furthered colonialist and capitalistic expansion. British expeditions had a distinct advantage over those from nations like Russia, France, and the United States in these endeavors because of its naval power and the territories and peoples that it had already claimed in the Southern Hemisphere. These contributed to British imperial networks, which Maddison describes as “circuits of necessity” due to the logistics required for excursions into polar waters; they enabled ships to use colonial outposts on islands throughout the Southern Hemisphere to restock provisions, carried out repairs and maintenance on ships and equipment, and replaced crew members, often through demonstrations of power (10; 22–54). “Circuits of necessity” enabled longer expeditions with fewer upfront costs as the British Empire expanded. This kind of colonial exploitation in pursuit of Antarctic territory increased into the twentieth century and continues in a neo-imperial sense today, as is evident in multi-disciplinary scholarship.6 Though much of the focus on Antarctic imperialism engages with early expeditions or the so-called “Heroic Age” of exploration (1895–1917), the institutions that were established in the mid-twentieth century for the administration of British interests in the South Atlantic derive from similar motivations as those of many earlier expeditions.7 For example, during the Second World War, interest in the South Atlantic increased significantly in part due to Germany’s attacks on Allied ships in the region. Additionally, Germany, Argentina, Chile, and the United States all conducted operations and made claims to parts of the Antarctic just prior to or during the war, and Britain responded in kind with Operation Tabarin. Tabarin established multiple bases in the Antarctic Peninsula (including, notably, Port Lockroy on Goudier Island) where men overwintered and carried out research and mapping surveys in the surrounding area. The operation became the Falkland Islands Dependencies Survey (FIDS) in 1945, which in turn became BAS in 1962.8 These iterations of the agency were overseen by the Colonial Office until 1967, at which point BAS was transferred to the Natural Environment Research Council. BAS remains invested in its own history, scientific work, and legacy. This commitment has driven many of its endeavors, including the decision to commission Davies, who is well-known in British art music for his symphonic output and environmental compositions (British Antarctic Survey, “Programme Notes for the Antarctic Symphony”; McLain, “A New Antarctic Symphony”). In 1995, amidst restoration work at Port Lockroy, BAS began the process of commissioning the symphony. BAS was looking for a high publicity project that would draw attention to British scientific endeavors in the region and that would interest the public in Antarctic history and ecology. The decision to approach Davies for the symphony commission was primarily rooted in his reputation for composing environmentalist and place-centric works and his high visibility in the British arts scene. Davies’s known interest in English composer Ralph Vaughan Williams (1872–1958) also contributed to the preference, as BAS was interested in commemorating Vaughan Williams’s music for Ealing Studios’ Scott of the Antarctic (1948) and his Sinfonia Antartica (1953), both of which they knew Davies to have seen and heard and found profoundly impactful (McLain, “A New Antarctic Symphony”; McLain, Letter to Freedman; BBC Radio Scotland, 1998).9 Davies and his manager, Judy Arnold, spent nearly a month in the Antarctic under the aegis of BAS as part of the commission. BAS captured documentary footage throughout the trip and arranged specific site excursions and interviews.
